# ⚕️ Project Sanctum- Instructions Guide

# **Project Sanctum- Instructions Guide** **(New Writer Version)**

# ---

 **Welcome\!**

You are joining a team of clinicians who guard the clinical simulations that frontier AI models are tested against.

You build the Worlds and design the Tasks within them — realistic patient cases with messy charts, conflicting specialist notes, and buried details, paired with clinical assignments an AI agent has to complete. You decide whether both are ready to teach an AI. Every scenario, every chart, every task, and every gold-standard response passes through your hands — and the ones that aren't strong enough don't move forward. Your decisions become the quality bar AI is held to.

Your success in this role is dependent on your clinical judgment and your eye for what makes a strong simulation. This document will teach you everything else. Read it carefully.

## **How to use this document**

This is your source of truth for Project Sanctum during your onboarding. It follows the same sequence as your workflow — read it front to back the first time, then use it as a reference.

***Estimated reading time:** \~30-40 min*

| Section | What It Covers | Reading Time Estimate |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **[Getting Started]()** | Setup, tools, policies | \~10 min |
| **[Project Overview]()** | What you're building and why | \~10 min |
| **[Phase 1 Part 1: Plan Your World]()** | Worlds, Tasks, Scenarios, Traps | \~20 min |

# 🚶 Getting Started: Admin Steps

## **Getting Started: Admin Steps**

Complete these in order before you do anything else:

1. **Accept your Mercor contract.** 

2. **Set up your Okta Dashboard.** Step-by-step guide [here](https://talent.docs.mercor.com/how-to/okta-access).  
   1. **Changing Names in Okta**: Once you login, go to settings and change display name. Make sure you select one of the last name options: either work\!  
   2. **Use the format: Name \- Specialty \- Role**  
      *For example: Joseph L \- Medicine \- Writer*

3. **Download Insightful** from the invite email you received. This is how your hours will be tracked once you are on the project. [Setup guide](https://talent.docs.mercor.com/how-to/use-insightful)

4. **Join Slack — you will be added automatically.**   
   1. **Locate the \#New-Writers channel and start a thread that you will use for all communication.**  
   2. **Use format: Name, Specialty, Level of training (Pgy number or attending), Goal Submission XX/XX**  
      Ex 1\. Joseph Lee, Pediatrics, attending, 05/28  
      Ex 2\. Joseph Lee, Radiology, pgy 3, 05/30  
        
5. **Sign in to RLS.** You may refer to the [RL Studio Guide](https://talent.docs.mercor.com/working/rl-studio-rls) for help.

# 🕰️ Your First 10 Hours

# **Your First 10 Hours on Sanctum** *(as of May 20, 2026\)*

**🚀 Why this first 10 hours matters**   
Project Sanctum is a **fast-paced healthcare AI project** running on 7 day build cycles. Most writer questions and drop-offs happen in this first 10-hour window, and it is the highest-friction part of the project. If something's going sideways, ping early. 

⏱ **Spread your hours across the week**  
Several stages depend on review feedback, and reviewers need \~24 hours to turn things around. 

📅 **Pacing expectations**  
Most writers complete the full path in less than a week. Each stage has a target window. Message your Onboarding EPM or TL if something's blocking you and we'll work with you on extenuating circumstances.

🎯 **End-of-week target**  
Approved World Spec Doc and onboarding complete\!

---

## **At a glance**

| Stage | Hours | By the end of this stage, you'll have… |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 1\. Setup | 0–3 | Tools set up, onboarding doc read, thread started |
| 2\. Brainstorming | 3–6 | Your first idea submitted and feedback incorporated |
| 3\. Spec Doc | 6–10 | A drafted and reviewed spec doc |

# 💻 AI usage Policy

# **How to Use Claude (and Other AIs) on This Project**

This page sets expectations for how Claude and other AIs (also known as **Large Language Models, LLM**) fit into your workflow on Project Sanctum. Read it before you start using Claude for any deliverable.

**•  Create a personal Claude account** and upgrade to the $20 Pro version. 

**•**  Post in the Slack Channel **\#incentives-bonuses-tracker** once paid to be reimbursed.  
You may use your personal email to bypass a known SSO blocker with mercor.expert emails.

**AI is a Tool, Not the Driver**

The use of Claude (or any LLM) should be a guide and accelerator — not the primary driver of what you create or submit. As emphasized in Office Hours: **you are the ultimate expert.** Everything that is generated — spec docs, world files, supporting documents — must be double- and triple-checked by you before it moves forward.

The reason the client has engaged us is precisely because we are physician specialists who can correct, improve, and train the LLM. That value is only delivered if we critically review every piece of LLM-assisted output before submission. **Skipping that step inverts the whole purpose of what we're doing here.**

##  **Signs We're Slipping into Rubber-Stamp Mode**

We're seeing patterns in recent submissions that suggest critical review is sometimes being skipped:

| Sign | What it looks like |
| :---: | ----- |
| **LLM-generated wording** | Generic phrasing, AI tells, voice that doesn't match a real clinician |
| **Timeline inconsistencies** | Dates or chronology that conflict within or across documents |
| **Typos and small errors** | Errors a careful read-through would have caught |

**These are exactly the kinds of issues you should be catching as the expert reviewer.**

**⚠️ If you're clearing your own QA in just a few minutes, that's a signal you may not be reviewing critically enough.** A proper critical review of LLM-assisted content takes real time.

##  **Non-Negotiables: 100% Human-Generated**

Three components of every task must be written by you, not by an LLM. LLMs can support world-building, but the evaluation core itself must come from the physician expert. This is the foundation of the entire project.

| 🚫 100% human-written (no exceptions) | ✅ LLM-assisted is OK |
| ----- | ----- |
| Task prompts | Brainstorming |
| Golden responses | Boilerplate / drafting templates |
| Grader guidelines | Consistency checking |

**There are no exceptions to these three.** LLMs can support world-building (brainstorming, boilerplate, consistency checking), but the evaluation core itself must come from the physician expert. This is the foundation of the entire project's integrity.

# ✈️ Project Overview

# **Project Overview**

---

## **Our Goal on Project Sanctum**

Your role on Project Sanctum is of a **senior clinician**. You bring three things that AI cannot: the **clinical instinct** to imagine a realistic patient case, the **skill** to produce work that meets senior clinician standards, and the **judgment** to evaluate output against those standards. Across the workflow, you will design patient scenarios, produce senior-quality clinical work, and evaluate AI output against those standards.

Here's what we're working toward: today's best AI models still cannot reliably perform senior-quality clinical work. Project Sanctum helps train these models by placing them inside **realistic simulations** of clinical work environments, where they must complete the kind of assignments a practicing clinician would handle in real life.

Each **World** is one of these simulations: a realistic patient case containing multiple clinical tasks and the patient chart a clinician like you would navigate to complete them. An **AI agent** will attempt each task using only the documents in that chart. You then produce the **Golden Response** — the industry-standard deliverable a senior clinician would arrive at — and the gap between the agent's output and your answer becomes the training signal used to improve future models. The more realistic the World, the more valuable that signal becomes.

A fully realistic patient chart with many files and materials would take you many hours to build by hand — and most of those hours would go into producing documents that follow familiar structural patterns. Sanctum is designed so that this large-scale production can be handled efficiently by AI, while you focus your time on shaping the case itself: defining the clinical context, structuring the tasks, and ensuring the resulting environment reflects the complexity and messiness of real clinical practice.

## **🤖  Working with AI on Project Sanctum**

Sanctum is a **Claude-collaborative** project from start to finish. Claude handles much of the heavy drafting — building documents, brainstorming first drafts, refining outputs — so the work is faster than doing everything by hand. Your job is **part designer**, **part reviewer**: you direct Claude on what to produce, and you own the quality of everything that leaves your hands. Only you know what's trivial in your practice area and what requires real senior judgment, and only you know what a realistic clinical assignment looks like in your specialty. The standard is professional ownership of the final product. 

For every deliverable, you will rely on AI Automated Quality Check findings (**AutoQC**, run automatically and surfaced to you) and targeted spot-checks instead of full read-throughs.

💡 **Two layers of quality checks**

* **AutoQC (required, formalized).** Every deliverable you submit runs through automated quality checks on the project’s platform. You job is to address each AutoQC flag — fix the issue or push back with reasoning if it's a false positive. No deliverable moves forward until its AutoQC findings are resolved.

* **Self-check with Claude (encouraged, informal).** Before uploading any deliverable, you're encouraged (not required) to run a manual checklist with Claude — like proofreading with Grammarly before submitting an essay. This catches obvious issues early so AutoQC doesn't have to flag them.

| ⚠  Your professional judgment overrides AI — always. Some writers fall into the trap of treating AI's suggestions as instructions: accepting AI's framing because it sounds confident, redirecting their thinking because AI pushed back, or rewriting their work to match AI's preferred version. Don't. You are the senior clinician; AI is the assistant working for you. When AI suggests a direction that contradicts your professional judgment, follow your judgment — and push back on the AI. The training data we're producing is only as valuable as the expertise leading every decision. |
| :---- |

| 💡  Our shared standards on Project Sanctum Realism — The scenarios, patient records, and clinical tasks you create should reflect what clinicians actually produce, work with, and complete in their day-to-day clinical practice. AI can only learn to do medical work if we train it on real medical work. Quality — AI models are only as strong as the data we give them. Your responsibility is making sure each deliverable is realistic and consistent with your World, using AutoQC \+ targeted spot-checks rather than full read-throughs. Attention to detail — The work is long, complex, and interconnected. AutoQC is embedded throughout this project to check and surface inconsistencies for you. Your job is to engage seriously with each finding: fix real issues, push back on false positives. The best experts treat AutoQC feedback as the trigger for their attention, not as something to skim past. Your judgment leads — When Claude suggests a direction that contradicts your professional judgment, follow your judgment. Claude doesn't know your clinical specialty; you do. Professionalism — You'll be reviewing each other's work, and disagreements will come up. Give each other the benefit of the doubt. When you flag a concern, be specific and constructive. When you receive feedback, engage with it seriously. When you and a reviewer disagree, escalate to a Team Lead with your reasoning — don't silently work around it. Direct, thoughtful dialogue is the norm here. |
| :---- |

## 

## **💡  The Driving Question**

| *How do I design a clinical environment that holds the workflows I’m required to complete, in a way that reflects the challenges of my day-to-day work and requires my expertise?* |
| :---: |

You know what professional-grade clinical work looks like — the format a senior clinician expects, the diagnostic depth patient safety requires, the judgment that comes from years of clinical practice. Think of the AI as someone just starting in your domain — freshly board-certified, or in their first year as a medical director — capable and knowledgeable, but without the seasoning that years in your specialty build. You're the seasoned one. The gap between someone just starting and someone seasoned is exactly the gap your tasks should expose.

## **The Three-Column Mental Model**

Three roles operate in parallel: the work you produce, what the AI does with it, and what we mean by "good." Hold all three columns in mind whenever you're designing.

| 1\. What you \+ AI produce | 2\. What the AI model does | 3\. What "good" means |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **A complete clinical environment package.** A realistic patient case (or multiple cases) and the surrounding clinical environment — including the scenario, multiple sources of information (EHR documents, patient-provided records, photos, external faxes, portal messages), patient records, and the clinical workflows that emerge from them. | An **AI Agent** attempts each clinical workflow by navigating the World files and working from the materials and instructions provided. | Everything you produce should be **realistic clinical work**, solvable by a strong clinician from the World files alone but too challenging for today's best AI to do well. |

## **The Three Core Concepts**

Three concepts form the spine of the project: Scenario, Task, and World. They build on each other in an order, and understanding how they relate is the foundation everything else rests on.

| Concept | What it is | How you establish it  |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **World** | The clinical environment you operate in — anchored in your role, your specialty, and the setting where you work. The World is the umbrella that holds your patient case, your clinical assignments, and the chart files the AI agent will navigate. | You start by naming your role ("I'm a hospitalist," "I'm a medical director in dermatology," "I'm an urgent care physician"). After your scenario and tasks are designed, the World *files* — the actual patient chart \+ any supporting documents — are generated and you review them before approving the build. |
| **Scenario** | A realistic patient case. It describes who the patient is, what their clinical situation is, and why care is happening now. | You brainstorm your patient case from your practice that fits your World — drawing from a case you'd realistically encounter in your role. |
| **Task** | A realistic clinical workflow an AI agent attempts to complete — the end-to-end work required to produce a specific deliverable (a discharge summary, a med reconciliation, a consult note, an RCA report). You'll design 8+ tasks per World, each mapped to one workflow on the approved list. | You sketch the 8+ workflows you'd realistically perform for that patient. |

## **Start with your role**

Before you brainstorm a scenario, sketch task ideas, or think about what materials or files belong in your World, anchor yourself in your role. Every clinician on this project comes in with a specialty and a setting — that's your starting point.

You might be a hospitalist managing inpatient admissions, a medical director reviewing peer cases, an urgent care physician handling walk-in evaluations, a dermatologist running an outpatient clinic, or a coding specialist auditing inpatient claims. Whatever your role is, that is the lens through which every design decision flows.

**Your role determines:**

* Which patient cases come to mind when you brainstorm your scenario

* Which workflows you'd realistically perform for that patient

* Which documents naturally exist in that working environment

* What "expert-quality" output looks like at the end

| 💡 A Simple Way to Think About this: 1\. Your role — "I am a \[specialty\] in \[setting\]." 2\. Your scenario — A patient case from my practice. 3\. Your tasks — The workflows I'd complete for that patient. 4\. Your World — The clinical environment that holds the case and supports the tasks. |
| :---- |

## **How a World Comes Together**

Here is the full sequence from start to finish. AI does the heavy drafting throughout; your role is to design, decide, and review.

| Make a plan                       ← design your scenario \+ task ideas        ↓ Build your World                  ← the patient chart \+ any additional materials                                       generated from your plan        ↓ Review the built World            ← confirm realism and complexity |
| :---- |

# ---

## **Part 1: Understanding how this project produces data**

Before you write a specification, you need to understand what you are building and why it matters. This part covers the fundamentals: what a world is, what goes in it, and how it connects to the tasks an AI agent will attempt. Master this first — the specification process in Part 2 builds directly on these concepts.

# ---

## **What is a World?**

Every task begins with a world — and each world supports 5–10 tasks.

| A world is a complete, self-contained file environment built around a single patient case. It is the workspace the AI agent operates in: the full set of clinical documents available to it when it attempts your tasks — progress notes, lab results, imaging reports, consult notes, medication lists, nursing assessments, discharge summaries, and outpatient records. |
| :---- |

Think of it this way: a world is a patient's complete chart. Every note, every lab, every consult, every order that would exist for that patient is in the chart. Nothing is flagged. Nothing is summarized for the agent. It has to figure out what matters, just like a physician would.

The agent has no information beyond what is in the world and what you tell it in the task prompt. Traps are not realistically and intentionally designed to simulate real-world points of friction. It cannot search UpToDate, call a specialist, or draw on anything outside the files you provide. Your job is to construct a clinical environment where the agent's reasoning can be rigorously tested — enough material for it to reach correct conclusions through careful reading and synthesis, but enough complexity, contradictory findings, and buried detail that doing so requires genuine clinical skill.

## 

## **What Goes Into A World?**

Now that you know what drives a world, here is what actually goes in it.

A world contains many documents. These are the clinical files the agent will have access to when it attempts your tasks. They should be the kinds of documents a physician working on your patient would actually encounter in an EMR — not a curated set of only the relevant ones, but a realistic chart that includes both essential files and realistic noise.

A world typically contains a mix of the following document types — the same kinds of files you would find in a real patient chart:

* **Progress notes** (daily attending notes, resident notes, overnight coverage notes) — the running narrative of the patient's hospital course, where key clinical decisions, exam findings, and plan changes are documented.

* **Lab results** (CBC, BMP, CMP, coagulation studies, trending values across days) — necessary for any task that requires tracking clinical trajectories or dosing decisions.

* **Imaging reports** (chest X-rays, CT scans, ultrasounds, MRIs) — where radiologic findings are interpreted, sometimes with discrepancies between preliminary and final reads.

* **Specialist consult notes** (cardiology, nephrology, GI, pulmonology, etc.) — where recommendations may conflict with each other or with the attending's final plan.

* **Medication lists and orders** (home medication lists, active inpatient orders, medication administration records, verbal orders) — the core of any reconciliation task, where copy-forward errors and ambiguity naturally accumulate.

* **Nursing documentation** (nursing flowsheets, vital signs, I/O records, nursing assessments) — adds granularity and realism, and may contain observations not reflected in physician notes.

* **Discharge and transfer documents** (discharge summaries, transfer notes, referral letters) — where information gets synthesized and where errors from earlier documentation often propagate.

* **Patient-provided documents** (handwritten medication lists, outside records, advance directives) — may contain inaccuracies that conflict with the chart.  
* 

* **Administrative documents** (insurance authorization forms, coding sheets, quality metric reports) — support healthcare administration tasks like prior auth, E/M coding, and HEDIS review.

# ---

## **What is a Scenario?**

| A scenario is the starting point of every world — the patient case that gives all the documents a reason to exist in one place. It describes the patient, their medical history, the admission event, and the clinical course that makes all tasks simultaneously active. |
| :---- |

A good scenario answers three questions:

**What is the clinical context?**  
The care setting, the reason for admission, and where the patient is in their hospital course? 

**Who are the key players?**  
The patient, their family, the attending, the consulting specialists, and the care team? 

**What is the precipitating event?**  
The single development (or cascade of complications) that makes all tasks simultaneously live?

Your scenario should be describable in a short paragraph. The world is everything that exists around it: the progress notes, lab results, imaging reports, consult notes, medication lists, and orders that a physician working on the case would have in the chart. You will build that full clinical document set in your World Spec.

The best patient profiles feel like someone you have actually taken care of. A colleague reading the chart should nod and say: "I've had this patient."

✅ **Strong Patient Example**

```
A 74-year-old male with CHF (EF 30%), CKD stage 3b, type 2 diabetes, atrial fibrillation on apixaban, GERD, and COPD. Admitted for CHF exacerbation, develops hospital-acquired AKI and upper GI bleed on day 3. Cardiology and Nephrology disagree on restarting ACE inhibitor and spironolactone. GI and IR disagree on bleed management. 11-day hospitalization with 26 home medications requiring reconciliation, then presents 2 weeks post-discharge to urgent care with a new complaint.
```

***Why this works:*** Common conditions interact in realistic ways. Every complication triggers medication changes. Specialist friction creates split decisions that prevent simple heuristics. The long stay generates a deep document trail with natural copy-forward errors.

**❌ Weak Patient Example**

```
A 28-year-old previously healthy female who presents with sudden-onset hemoptysis, found to have Goodpasture syndrome with concurrent anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis and pheochromocytoma.
```

**Why this fails:** Stacking three ultra-rare diagnoses tests trivia recall, not clinical reasoning. No meaningful trap opportunities, no polypharmacy, no specialist friction that mirrors real practice. If you need a zebra diagnosis to make a case hard, the case is contrived.

## **Designing Strong Patients**

Your patient is the foundation of the scenario — and the foundation of everything in your world. The best patient profiles feel like someone you have actually taken care of. A colleague reading the chart should nod and say: "I've had this patient."

Strong patient profiles typically feature:

* Multiple active comorbidities (10+) whose treatments interact  
* Polypharmacy (15+ medications) creating reconciliation complexity  
* Multi-day hospitalizations with specialist involvement and split decisions  
* Cascading complications where each problem triggers medication changes that affect the next  
* Realistic social and administrative complexities, such as fragmented documentation across multiple records, limited or unreliable history (e.g., foster care, estranged family), insurance or prior authorization barriers, care coordination challenges across systems, etc. 

## Complexity should emerge naturally from the intersection of common conditions — not from stacking rare diagnoses.

| *⚠️ Important:* Use fictional patients in your scenario. AI agents have access to training data. Using real patient cases from published literature or case reports creates a risk that the agent will draw on outside knowledge rather than reasoning from your World files. All patient names, dates, and identifying details must be fictional. To ensure names do not correspond to real individuals, err on the side of caution and use clearly fictional names. *Examples*: Johnny Elephante, Tommy Tambourine |
| :---- |

# ---

## **What Is a Task?**

You will not write tasks in Phase 1, but understanding what a task is will directly shape how you design your World — which files to include, what traps to embed, and how to scope your scenario.  
A task is the end-to-end representation of a legal workflow within a specific world and scenario.

| A task is a specific clinical request directed at an AI agent within a specific world and scenario. |
| :---- |

A task is a realistic clinical assignment that an AI agent attempts to complete using only the files in your World. Think of it as an instruction an attending might give a covering resident, or a workflow a care team needs completed during a hospitalization: reconcile these discharge medications, draft this consult note, complete this prior authorization. The agent receives your written prompt, accesses the World files, and attempts to produce the requested work product. It has no prior context about the patient beyond what is in the World and what you tell it in the prompt — think of it as a capable but uninstructed clinician sitting down to a chart for the first time.

Every task must meet three requirements:

1. **Represents real clinical work.** The task must be something a physician or clinical team member would actually perform: medication reconciliation, discharge summary drafting, consult note writing, diagnostic reasoning, coding determinations, and applying clinical guidelines.

2. **Produces a concrete, evaluable output.** A medication list, a discharge summary, a consult note, a coding determination, an authorization letter. If you cannot articulate what a correct output looks like, the task is not viable.

3. **Elicits model failure.** The agent's response must contain a material clinical deficiency. This is what makes the task useful for AI training.

| ✅ GOOD TASK EXAMPLE Workflow: Medication Reconciliation at Discharge Prompt: “I’m the covering resident preparing Mr. Pemberton for discharge after an 11-day admission for CHF exacerbation complicated by upper GI bleed and AKI. Please reconcile his discharge medication list using the attached documents.   Why this works: Real clinical work — medication reconciliation at discharge is a workflow physicians actually perform every day. Concrete, evaluable output — a medication list with annotations is a deliverable a grader can score against a defined standard. Elicits model failure — specialist disagreements about anticoagulation, a vague *"resume home meds"* order, and dose changes during AKI all create material opportunities for the model to make clinical errors. “Fair game” question — If you had asked 100 seasoned physicians this exact question and you have provided them with the world-level files necessary for self-containment, 95% of them would be able to complete the task satisfactorily without needing to ask follow up questions.  |
| :---- |

**Note**: There are additional elements in task prompts that make this strong. These prompt design principles are covered in detail in **[Task Prompt](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1yI-ixOoKAp7sfzSNIRttGdfTRKoE1pEt1XdKryoffkQ/edit?tab=t.xp659wfhtqsq)** section in Phase 2\. For now, focus on whether your task ideas meet the three requirements above; you'll learn to write the prompt itself in Phase 2\.

| ❌ BAD TASK EXAMPLE Workflow: General Clinical Question Prompt: “What medications should be stopped?” Why this fails: Not a real-world clinical deliverable \- Our questions have to simulate a real-world clinical deliverable from our list of [approved workflows](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1yI-ixOoKAp7sfzSNIRttGdfTRKoE1pEt1XdKryoffkQ/edit?tab=t.t5q7lmtajtoo). It is not clear what this is simulating from our list of clinical workflows.  Unclear ask — *"Should be stopped"* is ambiguous: Should be stopped when exactly? Today? Tomorrow? At discharge? Post-discharge?  Unlikely to yield model failure — The question does not provide enough room for nuance. Instead of asking for a medication discharge reconciliation list, which can include medications with dosage changes or new medications altogether, the question is too narrow and deterministic and thus increases the likelihood of the model getting the answer correct.  Not a “Fair game” question — If you had asked 100 seasoned physicians this question, the majority of them will have follow up questions. It would not be fair game for them to tackle this task and get it right on the first try because the question is framed poorly.  |
| :---- |

## **Why this matters for World Building**

Remember: your world exists to support **5–10 tasks**, and every design decision you make should be informed by the tasks you are contemplating. Four principles to keep in mind as you plan your World:

**Tasks must be answerable from the World files.** The agent can only work with what is in the World and what you tell it in the prompt. If a task requires a clinical finding, a lab value, or a medication order, the relevant document must be in the World.

**Good tasks require cross-document reasoning.** Tasks where the agent can succeed by pulling a single fact from a single document are not useful. This means your World files should distribute key information across multiple documents — the agent should have to find, connect, and synthesize to reach a correct answer.en

**The agent sees everything.** You cannot hide files from the agent. This means all World content must be logically consistent with your tasks. If something in the World contradicts a task, the agent will find it.

**Tasks should be diverse.** Your 5–10 tasks should span different clinical workflows, output types, and reasoning demands. This means your scenario needs to be broad enough — and your file set rich enough — to support a range of distinct assignments. A scenario that only supports one type of task is too narrow.

Detailed guidance on how to write task prompts, create golden responses, and prepare grading guidelines will be covered in a future phase.

# ---

## **What is a Trap**

| A trap is a deliberate point of friction embedded in your World files — a place where a careful reader would catch a problem but a less attentive one would not. Traps are not errors in your work. They are intentional design choices: a medication that was changed but never updated on the active list, two specialists who gave conflicting recommendations without resolution, a lab value from Day 1 that no longer applies on Day 8 but was never flagged as outdated. |
| :---- |

Traps live in the documents, never in the task prompt. The agent discovers them — or fails to — by reading the chart. This is exactly how real clinical risk works: the information is there, but finding it and acting on it correctly requires judgment.

A well-designed trap has three properties: it is clinically plausible (it could happen in a real chart), it is discoverable (the information needed to catch it exists in the World files), and it produces a meaningful error when missed (not a trivial formatting difference, but a clinical decision that changes).

## **The Most Common & Effective Trap Types**

| Trap Type | How It Works | Examples |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
|  **Copy-forward errors** | Outdated information carried forward across documents without being updated. Models tend to trust whatever appears most recently in the chart without checking whether it has been superseded. | *A pre-admission medication list still shows a drug discontinued during the hospitalization. The agent includes it on the discharge list.* |
| **Specialist friction** | Conflicting recommendations from different services, with a split attending decision. The correct answer requires tracing the disagreement to the attending's final decision. | *Cardiology recommends restarting lisinopril; Nephrology recommends holding it; the attending sides with Nephrology. The agent follows the most recent consult note instead of the attending's decision.* |
| **Temporal contamination** | Information from the wrong time point mixed into the current context. Models tend to treat all documents as contemporaneous. | *Day-1 lab values used to make a day-11 decision, or a discharge summary included in a file set for a task anchored to day 7\.* |
| **Authority ambiguity** | Unclear which source should take precedence when documents conflict. | *A verbal attending order contradicts the most recent progress note, or a resident's plan differs from the specialist's recommendation without documented resolution.* |
| **Resume order traps** | A vague "resume home medications" order in the context of a patient who had multiple medication changes during the admission. | *The patient had 8 medication changes during admission. The correct answer requires full reconciliation, not execution of the shorthand order.* |
| **Patient-provided inaccuracy** | A patient or family member provides a document that conflicts with the chart. The model must recognize the conflict, not simply defer to whichever it reads last. | *An outpatient pharmacy record contradicts the patient's notes on their phone. A daughter brings a handwritten medication list including discontinued drugs and missing new ones.* |

## **What Separates a Strong Trap from a Weak One**

The table above tells you what kinds of traps to build. This section shows you the difference between a trap that works and one that does not.

| ❌Weak trap: Single-file, single-error A lab report lists potassium as 5.8 mEq/L, but the progress note from the same day documents it as 4.2 mEq/L. Why this is weak: The discrepancy lives between only two documents and involves a simple numerical mismatch. The agent can catch it by comparing one value against another — no clinical reasoning required. This is a data-checking task, not a clinical judgment task. |
| :---- |

| Weak trap: Bypassable with general knowledge The world files include a medication order for metformin in a patient whose most recent creatinine is 3.2. The trap relies on the agent knowing that metformin is contraindicated in severe renal impairment. Why this is weak: Any model with access to general medical knowledge or web search can flag this. The trap tests factual recall, not chart navigation or synthesis. The agent does not need to engage deeply with your world files to get this right. |
| :---- |

| Strong trap: Cross-document synthesis required A cardiology consult on Day 3 recommends starting anticoagulation with apixaban. A nephrology consult on Day 5 notes declining renal function and recommends dose-adjusting all renally cleared medications — but does not specifically mention apixaban. The pharmacy medication list on Day 6 still shows the original apixaban dose. The discharge summary task requires medication reconciliation. Why this is strong: The agent must find the cardiology recommendation, connect it to the nephrology note's general guidance about renal dosing, recognize that apixaban is renally cleared, notice that the pharmacy list was never updated, and determine the correct adjusted dose. This requires reading across at least four documents and applying clinical reasoning to connect them. A model that only reads the pharmacy list will produce an incorrect reconciliation. |
| :---- |

| Strong trap: Conflicting specialist recommendations A pulmonology consult recommends continuing high-dose corticosteroids for an acute COPD exacerbation. An endocrinology consult from the same day recommends tapering steroids urgently due to worsening hyperglycemia and early steroid-induced myopathy. Neither consult references the other. The task asks the agent to write a discharge plan that addresses both the pulmonary and endocrine management. Why this is strong: There is no single correct answer that satisfies both specialists' recommendations simultaneously. The agent must identify the conflict, weigh the competing risks, and justify a clinical approach. A model that follows one consult without acknowledging the other will produce a flawed discharge plan. |
| :---- |

| Strong trap: Temporal reasoning across the admission timeline A patient is started on vancomycin on Day 1\. A trough level drawn on Day 3 comes back elevated. The pharmacist recommends holding the next dose in a note buried in the pharmacy section. The Day 4 nursing medication administration record shows the dose was still given. The Day 5 labs show a further rise in trough level plus a new acute kidney injury. The task asks the agent to document an adverse drug event analysis. Why this is strong: The agent must reconstruct a timeline across pharmacy notes, nursing records, and lab results spanning five days. The critical failure point — the dose that should have been held — is documented in a pharmacy note that is easy to overlook if the agent does not systematically review all medication-related documents in chronological order. |
| :---- |

**Check your traps against these questions:**

**Does solving this trap require reading three or more documents?** If the agent can catch it from one or two files, it is probably too easy.

**Would a model with strong general medical knowledge but no access to the chart still get it wrong?** If general knowledge is sufficient, the trap is not testing chart navigation.

**Is the plausible wrong answer something a careful but imperfect reader might actually produce?** If the wrong answer is obviously absurd, the trap has no teeth.

**Does the trap arise naturally from the clinical scenario, or does it feel artificially inserted?** Traps woven into the patient's story are stronger than traps that require inventing unrealistic errors.

# ---

## **How Do They Connect?**

The four core concepts you just learned — World, Scenario, Task, and Trap — form a single design chain. Each one shapes the next:

Your **scenario** defines the patient case — who the patient is, what happened, and why everything is active at once. It is the reason all the documents in your World exist in one place.

Your **World** is the complete clinical environment built around that scenario. It contains every document the AI agent will have access to — and nothing else. The agent cannot look beyond the World, so the World must contain everything needed to answer your tasks.

Your **tasks** are the clinical assignments the agent attempts using the World files. Each task tests whether the agent can do real clinical work: find the right documents, interpret them correctly, and produce a defensible output. The tasks are what give the World its purpose — without tasks, the World is just a collection of files.

## Your **traps** are what make the tasks genuinely difficult. They live in the World files, not in the task prompt. A copy-forwarded medication list, a specialist recommendation the attending overruled, a lab value from the wrong day — the agent has to discover the problem by reading carefully, the same way an attentive physician would.

![][image8]

The design process is not purely linear — your trap ideas may cause you to adjust your patient's comorbidities or clinical course, your task ideas will shape which files you need, and the files you have access to may change which tasks are viable. Expect to iterate.

## **What Makes A World Realistic?**

| Property | What It Means | Ask Yourself |
| :---: | ----- | ----- |
| **Realism** | The scenario, documents, and tasks reflect how clinical work actually happens — including the messiness, information gaps, and moments where judgment is required. | Would a physician look at this chart and recognize it as realistic? |
| **Difficulty** | The difficulty comes from the documents and from applying domain knowledge to those documents — not from trick wording in the prompt. | Is this hard because of the medicine, or hard because the prompt is confusing? |
| **Evaluability** | Every task produces a concrete output that can be graded. If you cannot articulate what a correct answer looks like, the task is not suitable. | Can I write a definitive correct answer for every task in this world? |

Of these three, **realism** is the most important. A World that feels contrived is not useful, even if it produces difficult tasks. Your documents should look like something a physician would actually find in a patient chart, not materials arranged to manufacture a specific outcome.

**Difficulty** should emerge naturally from the complexity of the clinical scenario and the documents, not from rare diagnoses or deliberately confusing file organization. If your World requires the agent to reconcile conflicting specialist recommendations, trace medication changes across a multi-day hospitalization, and synthesize findings from progress notes, lab trends, and consult notes, the difficulty will take care of itself.

**Evaluability** is your design constraint: every task you plan for this World must produce a concrete output that can be graded. If you find yourself thinking "there's no right answer to this," either rethink the task or adjust the World files until a defensible answer becomes articulable.

## 

## 

##

Before moving to Part 2 (Writing Your World Specification), confirm every item:

| Can you explain what a world is in one sentence? Can you describe the difference between a Scenario and a World? Can you explain why understanding Tasks matters for World Building, even though you won't write them in this phase? Do you know what makes a World realistic? (Realism, Difficulty, Evaluability) Can you describe what goes into a World, including clinical document types and the difference between essential and supplementary files? Can you define what a trap is and name at least three of the five trap types? Do you understand why no single file should give the agent everything it needs? Do you know what makes a bad trap? (prompt inconsistency, inappropriate versioning, over-authoritative summaries) Do you understand how the four core concepts connect? (Scenario creates World, World contains files, files support Tasks, traps make Tasks hard) |

# 🔄 RLS Workflow

**STUDIO WORKFLOW GUIDE**

**World Planning and Brainstorming**

*Step-by-step reference for new and returning writers*

**Please begin by watching the [step-by-step video guide](https://mercor.enterprise.slack.com/files/U0A6X7K7PSN/F0B519PPCTC/studio_world_planning_and_brainstorming_workflow.mp4).**

This guide walks through the brainstorming and world planning workflow in RL Studio (RLS). Previously this work was done in Airtable or Google Docs only; moving forward, every stage lives in RL Studio. The guide is written primarily for new writers, but veterans will find the workflow reference useful as well.  
For help accessing RL Studio, please follow these instructions: [RL Studio Guide.](https://talent.docs.mercor.com/working/rl-studio-rls)

The workflow has two sequential stages, each gated by human review:

1. **Brainstorming / Planning** — upload your planning document.

2. **World Spec Drafting** — upload the full spec.

| The golden rule: AutoQC must be run at every stage, and all valid feedback must be addressed before submitting for human review. AutoQC improves over time, and skipping it is the most common cause of rework. |
| :---- |

# **Stage 1: Brainstorming and Planning**

## **1.1 Get into the right world**

After logging into RL Studio, accept the invite to the **Live World Creation and Planning** world. This is where all task phases for world planning and brainstorming take place.

* Left handside: Dashboards \> My World Building Tasks  
* Confirm drop down \=  \[LIVE\] World Creation and Planning 

## **1.2 Create your task**

1. Click **Create Task**.

2. You'll now be in the drafting view, where you can create or upload your brainstorm, run AutoQC, and submit for review.

3. Select your Pod as New/Onboarding

## **1.3 Upload your brainstorming document**

1. Click **Upload**.

2. Select your brainstorming/planning document from your computer.

3. Confirm the upload completed.

## **1.4 Run AutoQC**

1. Click to run AutoQC on the uploaded document.

2. Wait for the results to populate. You can also view results under the **AutoQC** section of the task — note that the WorldSpec AutoQC option shown here is for the next stage and won't fetch anything useful yet.

3. Review every item AutoQC returns:

* **Valid feedback** — make the change in your document, re-upload, and re-run AutoQC to confirm the fix is sufficient.

* **Feedback you disagree with** — write down notes explaining why, so you have a clear answer if a reviewer asks about it.

*Running AutoQC and reviewing the results is required before submitting. Do not skip this step.*

## **1.5 Mark diagnostics reviewed and submit**

1. Once you've worked through all AutoQC results, click **Mark Diagnostics Reviewed**.

2. Submit your plan for review.

The task status will move from **Plan Drafting** to **Ready for Plan Review**.

## **1.6 What happens during review**

* **Ready for Plan Review** — waiting for a reviewer to pick it up.

* **In Progress** — a reviewer is actively reviewing.

* **Approved** — you can move on to World Spec Drafting (Stage 2).

* **Needs Fixes** — the reviewer has comments to address.

## **1.7 Handling “Needs Fixes”**

1. Open the task and read the reviewer's feedback (visible directly in RL Studio).

2. Click **Start Plan Fixes** to return to drafting.

3. Delete the old document if needed, upload the revised version.

4. Re-run AutoQC.

5. Resubmit.

| Communication tip: All feedback should be communicated in RL Studio so everything is tracked in one place. Slack is fine for quick back-and-forth with your reviewer to speed things up, but the official feedback record lives in RL Studio. |
| :---- |

# **Stage 2: World Spec**

NOTE: do not continue in RL Studio to draft your world spec. See the “World Spec documentation” tab to review how to draft your world spec. This stage here only refers to once you’ve already got your world spec drafted (covers how to upload and run in RL studio). 

Once your brainstorming document is approved, the task status becomes **Ready for Spec Drafting**.

## **2.1 Start the stage**

1. Click into the task.

2. You'll now see your approved brainstorming document from the previous stage available for reference, plus an option to upload a World Spec document.

3. Click **Start Spec Drafting**.

## **2.2 Upload spec and template/reference files**

1. Upload your World Spec document.

2. Upload any template/reference files needed for the spec (used by the engineering team to create synthetic files for your world).

## **2.3 Run AutoQC (again, and seriously this time)**

Run the spec-stage AutoQC. This one is particularly reliable — if there are issues here that you don't address, **you will almost certainly receive reviewer feedback about them**. Save yourself the round-trip:

* Work through every flagged issue.

* Re-upload and re-run AutoQC until clean (or you have documented disagreement).

* Mark diagnostics reviewed.

## **2.4 Submit for spec review**

Submit. The review process is identical to Stage 1:

* **Ready for Spec Review** — waiting

* **In Progress** — reviewer is working on it

* **Approved** — move to pipeline stage

* **Needs Fixes** — click **Start Spec Fixes**

## **2.5 Handling spec fixes**

When fixes are needed, the fix view shows **both** the planning-stage feedback from Stage 1 **and** the current spec-stage reviewer feedback. Work through them, upload your updated documents, run AutoQC, and resubmit.

That completes the workflow for onboarding\!

**Quick Reference: Task Statuses**

| Status | What it means | What you do |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Plan Drafting** | You're working on the brainstorm | Upload, run AutoQC, submit |
| **Ready for Plan Review** | Submitted, waiting | Wait |
| **Plan In Progress** | Reviewer is working on it | Wait |
| **Needs Plan Fixes** | Reviewer has comments | Start Plan Fixes, address feedback, resubmit |
| **Ready for Spec Drafting** | Plan approved | Start Spec Drafting |
| **Spec In Progress / Needs Spec Fixes** | Same pattern as plan | Same pattern as plan |
| **Spec Doc Approved**  | Ready for a Pod | Wait for EPM |

# **Things That Will Save You Time**

* **Run AutoQC at every stage.** It catches the exact issues reviewers will flag.

* **Address every valid AutoQC item before resubmitting.** Re-run AutoQC after edits to confirm.

* **Document any AutoQC items you disagree with.** A short note is enough.

* **Follow the naming conventions** from the onboarding guide when setting up workspaces.

* **Keep feedback in RL Studio** as the source of truth, but use Slack with your reviewer for fast clarification.

* **Ask in Slack** if anything is unclear. New writers especially benefit from working closely with their reviewer.

# 🧠 Brainstorm Your World

# **Before Your Start: Brainstorm Your World**

**World Brainstorm Checkpoint**

*Conceptual sign-off before world spec drafting begins*

## **Purpose**

This checkpoint exists so you do not invest weeks in a full world spec built on a foundation that will not hold up. The bar at this stage is conceptual viability, not spec quality. The lead is signing off on "this idea is worth building out," not on "this is a finished design."

Output of the checkpoint is binary: go or send back. If sent back, the writer revises the brainstorm and re-presents.

# **What the writer brings**

A brainstorm in either bullet or short narrative form, covering the four elements below. No file inventories, no document drafts, no full timeline yet. This is a concept pitch.

# 🎨 Brainstorm Template

**Brainstorm Template** 

*NOTE: Feel free to slightly modify as you see fit*

| Element | What to bring | Examples |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **1\. World setup** | Who the patient is and what clinical situation the world represents: •  Demographics and comorbidities •  Clinical environment (specialty, inpatient vs. outpatient vs. administrative oversight) •  Encounter type (admission, clinic visit, RCA review, peer review, coding audit, and so on) •  Shape of the timeline; what changes over the course of the world Enough to know the world is medically and contextually coherent. | *"This is an inpatient hospital medicine world: a \[N\]-day admission for \[presenting problem\] in a \[age\] \[sex\] with \[comorbidities\]."* *"This is an outpatient primary care world: a single clinic visit for \[chief complaint\] in a \[age\] \[sex\] with \[relevant chronic conditions\]."* *"This is a medical director world: an RCA review of \[event type\] involving a \[age\] \[sex\] who \[outcome\]; reviewer has access to chart and incident materials."* |
| **2\. Major friction points** | Opposing forces, viewpoints, or stakeholder positions that complicate the scenario: •  Two specialists with conflicting recommendations •  Family wishes vs. medical recommendation •  Primary team vs. consultant disagreement Frictions are about people and perspectives. Traps (next row) are about information. | *"Cardiology and nephrology disagree on whether to hold the ACE inhibitor."* *"Family wants comfort care; the primary team is still pursuing aggressive workup."* *"PCP recommends one regimen at clinic; the inpatient team has a different plan at admission."*  |
| **3\. Major traps** | Nuggets of information or specific incidents that complicate the clinician's job and can lead to incorrect decisions if not contextualized properly.  **Common trap types:** •  Contradictory EMR information •  Buried clinically significant information •  Insufficient or missing patient information •  Source-of-truth ambiguity •  Social determinants of health •  Temporal or sequencing complexity | *"Stale EMR med list contradicts a recently filled pill bottle photo. Source-of-truth ambiguity. Lives in the med rec task only."* *"Aspiration event documented mid-paragraph in a routine nursing note, never escalated. Buried significant information. World-level trap."* *"Caregiver burnout limits adherence and follow-up capacity. SDOH trap. World-level, affects every task that touches the discharge plan."* |
| **4\. Rough task ideas** | The clinical workflows the writer is thinking about as task encounters. Each task is independent and lives temporally after the world. For each task: the deliverable type and which world elements, traps, or frictions it would test. **Reference the team's approved workflows tracker** for the full list of validated deliverable types. The categories below are a representative sample to encourage thinking beyond progress notes and discharge medication lists. •  Direct clinical documentation (H\&P, progress note, discharge summary, consult, SOAP, op note) •  Medication, coding, & billing (med rec, ICD-10/CPT crosswalk, prior auth, denial appeal) •  Care transitions & coordination (transfer note, post-discharge follow-up, home health plan, hospice/palliative) •  Quality, safety, & oversight (RCA, sentinel event, M\&M, peer review, OPPE/FPPE, utilization review) •  Administrative-clinical hybrid (FMLA, disability, ADA accommodation, return-to-work, workers' comp, SAP) •  Specialty evaluation & legal-medical (VA disability, SSDI, IME, pre-op clearance, school medical form) | *"Task 1 is a discharge medication reconciliation. Draws on the three-way med discrepancy and the buried dose change. Set at hospital day 7, which is the final day of the world."* *"Task 2 is a pre-operative clearance note. Draws on the cardiology/nephrology friction and the chronic disease profile. Set 2 weeks after the last day of the clinical timeline (discharge date)."* *"Task 3 is the RCA write-up itself (medical director world). Draws on every friction and trap. Set 4 weeks after the index event."* |

## 

## **What the lead evaluates**

Walk through the checklist below, organized to mirror the writer's four elements. Send back if any item is a clear no.

| World setup Patient and clinical situation are coherent. The patient/scenario could exist; specialty, environment, encounter type, and timeline are clear and internally consistent. Patient profile fits the encounter. Realistic in the sense that a domain expert has encountered this patient several times in their career. Major friction points Frictions realistically represent real-world clinical dilemmas. Writer can name the stakeholders involved and what each is advocating for. Major traps There are a variety of traps in the world that altogether create enough clinical complexity that can stump a physician under normal circumstances. Rough task ideas Each task maps to a deliverable type in the team's approved workflows tracker. Tasks also have their own “traps” that are distinct from the world-level traps.  Cross-cutting Writer has answers for potential issues of self-containment that can arise.  A seasoned clinician could solve every task from the intended files alone. Overall world design is representative of the daily activities of a physician in that domain.  |
| :---- |

# 

## **Decision**

| GO Foundation is viable. Writer proceeds to full spec drafting. | SEND BACK At least one viability check is a clear no. Lead notes which items need revisiting. Writer revises and re-presents. |
| :---: | :---: |

Sign-off is verbal or in a brief comment. No formal write-up required at this stage.

# 💼 Selecting Workflows

# **Selecting Workflows**

Each world should contain 5–10 tasks spanning different clinical workflows. 

**The list of workflows can be found here:**

**[ Task Selection Categories For Team](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1YRUwLm3oLjlL2v2g-_lw9rC_NeJ5gcpHBX6_M_HHh4c/edit?gid=668143205#gid=668143205)**

From that grouping, you choose which 5–10 to include as tasks in your world. 

Refer to the sheet above to see the recommended task and workflows that you will be simulating and designing for this project. Note that some are prioritized over the others (P0 \= high priority, P1 \= medium priority, P2 \= low priority)

***Start with P0 workflows – these are the current priority.***  
***P1 and P2 workflows are also acceptable if P0 workflows are exhausted***

In practice, you have to wear multiple hats as physicians. Your day-to-day life can vary and consists of responsibilities that could be purely clinical in nature vs. healthcare admin focused vs. educational vs. a combination of all of the above. The “deliverables” you are routinely producing in the inpatient and outpatient settings range from writing progress notes and discharge summaries to reviewing quarterly reports for physician productivity and coding compliance.

**Tasks per world: rules of thumb**

* **Total tasks per world:** 5–10  
* **Distinct workflows per world:** at least 3–5  
* **Workflow repetition is allowed** — you can use the same workflow multiple times within a world, as long as the minimum of 3–5 distinct workflows is met overall.

**Example:** A world with 8 tasks could look like this:

🔸 3 tasks → Ambulatory Clinical Progress Note Documentation (SOAP Notes)

🔸 2 tasks → Discharge Medication Reconciliation

🔸 2 tasks → Prior Authorization Request and Management

🔸 1 task → Hospital Discharge Summary Generation

That's 4 distinct workflows across 8 tasks — SOAP notes are repeated 3x, which is fine because the overall workflow count clears the minimum.

**Task Anchoring**

Every task in your world must be anchored at a date that comes **after the latest document in your world**.

**Rules**

* The world files define a fixed clinical history. Every task takes place **after** that history ends.  
* No task may be set **within or in between** the dates of existing world files. If your world's last document is dated June 5, no task can be dated June 4 or earlier, and no task can fall between any two existing world file dates.  
* Think of each task as a future clinical episode for this patient: a follow-up clinic visit, a re-admission, a specialist consult, a discharge summary, a transition of care note. These are encounters that occur after the existing world chart.

**Quick check:** open your world spec, find the most recent document date, and confirm every one of your tasks is anchored after that date. If any task falls before or between existing dates, rework it before submission.

**Task Independence**

Every task in your world must function as a fully **independent clinical scenario**. The agent does not carry context across tasks — each task is evaluated on its own, with the world serving as the shared clinical backdrop.

**Rules**

* Task 3 cannot assume the agent completed Task 1 first.  
* Each task must stand on its own as a complete clinical scenario.  
* Tasks do not need to be chronologically ordered with each other.  
* Different tasks can represent different "parallel universes" of what happens to the patient after the world ends.

**Example**

If your world's last document is dated June 5, valid tasks could include any of the following — in any combination, in any order:

* **Task A — June 6:** Discharge summary for the admission described in the world  
* **Task B — June 9:** ED visit for an unrelated issue  
* **Task C — June 10:** Re-admission for a related complication  
* **Task D — July 1:** Ambulatory follow-up visit

**Key principle:** these tasks do not share a single timeline. They branch outward from the world in different directions and represent different possible futures for the patient.

# 🧠 Brainstorm Ex. 2

| WORLD BRAINSTORM CHECKPOINT *Conceptual sign-off before world spec drafting begins* World \[number per tracker\]  |  Pre-Deployment Travel Medicine: Immunosuppressed Contract Healthcare Worker  |  Project Sanctum |
| :---- |

*Concept pitch only. The bar at this stage is conceptual viability, not spec quality. Output is binary: GO or SEND BACK. Specific diagnoses, drug names, doses, ages, dates, and destination are design proposals fixed at spec time against source materials.*

# **1\. World Setup**

Typical clinical world. An academic travel medicine and preventive medicine clinic that also delivers some primary care. The writer is the acting department medical director while the permanent director is on leave, which seeds one program-level oversight task within this clinical world.

Anchor patient: a woman of childbearing potential, foreign-born and BCG-vaccinated at birth, working as a US-based contract or locums registered nurse. She is being prepared and cleared for a short-term international clinical deployment to a yellow-fever-endemic, high-tuberculosis-burden destination with a highland-plus-lowland itinerary (altitude and a malaria risk gradient). Multi-system but bounded: Crohn disease maintained on an anti-TNF biologic (the immunosuppression engine), latent tuberculosis risk with prior BCG (the screening-confounder engine), and well-controlled type 2 diabetes on metformin (the fitness and medication-logic engine). Pregnancy status is deliberately unresolved at intake.

Timeline shape: a longitudinal pre-departure arc anchored on a fixed deployment departure date, running from screening and referral through pre-departure clearance, with an optional post-deployment return touchpoint. Tasks are independent encounters along this arc; the arc is shared substrate, not a continuous story tasks build on.

# **2\. Major Friction Points**

*Two central, two secondary. Frictions are people and perspectives.*

* **Central. Patient versus clinician on vaccines and screening (semi-informed).** The patient is a nurse who arrives pre-loaded with conclusions drawn from an AI chatbot and social media. She advocates skipping yellow fever protection and dismissing tuberculosis screening (“my skin test is always positive, it is just the BCG”). The clinician advocates accurate risk mitigation: the chatbot is partially right about the contraindication but wrong about the consequence. Sharp because she half-knows the literature.

* **Central. Staffing agency occupational health versus clinician on evidence-based screening.** The agency protocol demands a tuberculin skin test plus an annual chest x-ray for every deployed worker regardless of BCG history, and withholds clearance without them. The clinician advocates IGRA given the BCG confounder and argues a repeat chest x-ray is not indicated absent symptoms or a positive IGRA, especially with a recent normal film.

* **Secondary. Entry-requirement and agency insistence on yellow fever proof versus clinical contraindication.** The destination entry framework and the agency require documented yellow fever vaccination. The clinician holds that the live vaccine is contraindicated by the biologic and must issue a medical exemption with risk counseling and possible itinerary modification.

* **Secondary. Treating gastroenterology versus travel and preventive clinic on biologic and latent TB timing.** Gastroenterology advocates maintaining remission and continuing the biologic uninterrupted. The travel and preventive clinician advocates that latent tuberculosis must be addressed before or alongside continued anti-TNF given deployment to a high-burden setting, which creates a real sequencing tension against the fixed departure date.

# **3\. Major Traps**

*Traps are information. Type, one-line description, source location, world-level or task-level.*

* **Source-of-truth ambiguity.** CDC, WHO, and the destination entry requirement disagree on yellow fever for the itinerary, while the biologic independently contraindicates the live vaccine; correct path is exemption plus risk mitigation, not vaccinate. Source: travel guidance reference excerpts in world files. World-level.

* **Contradictory records.** A historical positive tuberculin skin test (read as “positive, BCG”) sits against the indicated IGRA; anchoring on the skin test or treating BCG as exculpatory both fail, and anti-TNF raises the reactivation stakes. Source: prior occupational health record and outside chart. World-level.

* **Buried significant information and temporal.** The biologic last-dose date and latent TB treatment plan are buried in a gastroenterology or infusion record, and must be reconciled against the fixed departure date. Source: GI/infusion note in world files. World-level.

* **Insufficient information requiring acknowledged uncertainty.** Pregnancy status is not clearly documented near the consult; the live vaccine and chemoprophylaxis decisions hinge on it; the correct answer requires resolution before action, not assumption. Source: intake and nursing note ambiguity. World-level.

* **Buried significant information.** The base site is high-altitude and low malaria risk while a field excursion to a lowland area in the itinerary creates real risk; the detail is buried in agency deployment paperwork and agent selection is constrained by immunosuppression, T2DM, childbearing potential, and cost. Source: agency deployment itinerary document. World-level.

* **Source-of-truth ambiguity (low-tier noise).** A patient-introduced AI chatbot screenshot asserts a plausible but partially wrong claim in an authoritative voice; it must be subordinated in the source hierarchy and never carries any fact a correct answer needs. Source: patient-provided document, single task only. Task-level.

# **4\. Rough Task Ideas**

*Five tasks, four clinical and administrative plus one program-level director task. Standard spec is five; the director thread is one of them. Each maps to an approved workflow category and carries task-level traps distinct from world-level traps.*

**Task 1\. Pre-travel consultation note**

Deliverable type: Direct clinical documentation.

World elements drawn on: Yellow fever guidance discordance, live-vaccine versus immunosuppression, malaria itinerary and altitude, unresolved pregnancy status, the semi-informed vaccine-hesitancy friction, the GI versus travel friction.

Task-level traps: The single patient-introduced AI artifact lives here; plus a destination entry-requirement detail buried in agency paperwork that the consult must address as exemption rather than rubber-stamp.

Timeline anchor: Roughly six to eight weeks before the fixed departure date, to allow vaccine timing and latent TB lead time.

**P0: Ambulatory Visit Note Generation (SOAP Notes))** 

**Task 2\. Letter to staffing agency occupational health: TB screening interpretation and latent TB management**

Deliverable type: Care transitions and coordination (interagency communication).

World elements drawn on: BCG versus IGRA contradiction, buried biologic timing, the agency versus clinician friction, the GI versus travel friction.

Task-level traps: A recent normal chest x-ray report in the record against the agency demand for another (over-testing); an IGRA result requiring careful interpretation, including the realistic possibility of an indeterminate result under immunosuppression.

Timeline anchor: Roughly five to six weeks before departure, after the consult referral and before clearance.

**(P0: Specialist Referral Documentation)** 

**Task 3\. Fitness-for-deployment clearance letter**

Deliverable type: Specialty evaluation and legal-medical (fitness-for-duty).

World elements drawn on: The occupational sub-framework, all three comorbidities, the yellow fever medical exemption, the agency versus clinician friction.

Task-level traps: An agency clearance form whose checkbox criteria conflict with clinical reality (for example, “fully immunized per schedule” cannot be truthfully attested given the contraindication), forcing a documented medically accurate exception rather than a rubber stamp.

Timeline anchor: Roughly two to three weeks before departure.

**(P0: Specialist Referral Documentation)** 

**Task 4\. Medication reconciliation and travel medication plan**

Deliverable type: Medication, coding, and billing (medication reconciliation).

World elements drawn on: Multi-source reconciliation, buried biologic last-dose timing, chemoprophylaxis constraints, T2DM medication logic.

Task-level traps: Infusion-center record, patient-reported list, and primary care list disagree on the biologic agent, dose, or interval, or on the metformin dose; a drug or condition interaction buried in the chemoprophylaxis selection (including childbearing-potential constraints).

Timeline anchor: Roughly three to four weeks before departure.

**(P0: Medication Reconciliation Documentation)** 

**Task 5\. Medical director program-level review**

Deliverable type: Quality, safety, and oversight (focused utilization and safety review memo).

World elements drawn on: This patient as the sentinel case for a department-level review of pre-deployment TB screening practice and live-vaccine screening in immunosuppressed travelers, including unnecessary chest x-rays driven by agency protocol. Program-level analysis, not re-adjudication of the individual.

Task-level traps: Aggregate data with a confounded denominator or a misattributed near-miss; a scope-discipline trap tempting the writer to re-litigate the individual case rather than produce program-level findings; a self-containment firewall preventing import of Tasks 1 through 4 conclusions as given.

Timeline anchor: Roughly four to six weeks after the patient deploys (retrospective review window).  
**(P0: Patient Safety Event Investigation and Root Cause Analysis)** 

# **What the Lead Evaluates**

*Walk the checklist. Send back if any item is a clear no.*

| Area | Checks |
| :---- | :---- |
| World setup | Patient and clinical situation are coherent; specialty, environment, encounter type, and timeline are clear and internally consistent. Patient profile fits the encounter and is one a domain expert has seen several times. |
| Major friction points | Frictions represent real-world clinical dilemmas; stakeholders and what each advocates are named. |
| Major traps | Variety of traps that together create enough complexity to stump a physician under normal circumstances. |
| Rough task ideas | Each task maps to an approved workflow deliverable type; each has its own traps distinct from world-level traps. |
| Cross-cutting | Self-containment is achievable and the writer has answers; a seasoned clinician could solve every task from intended files alone; the world is representative of daily activities in the domain. |

| GO Foundation is viable. Writer proceeds to full spec drafting. | SEND BACK At least one viability check is a clear no. Lead notes which items need revisiting. Writer revises and re-presents. |
| :---- | :---- |

*Sign-off is verbal or in a brief comment. No formal write-up required at this stage.*

# ✅ Brainstorm Checklist

**PROJECT SANCTUM**

**Brainstorm Checklist**

| The 4 brainstorm sections (the whole template) |
| :---- |

**☐**  World Setup — Setting (inpatient/outpatient/admin), specialty, age/sex, comorbidities, clinical course. One paragraph.

**☐**  Major Friction Points — At least 2 stakeholder conflicts (people, not info gaps). E.g. ID vs Cards

**☐**  Major Traps — Describe each with location and trigger mechanism. Aim for 5+ types. Note world-level vs task-only.

**☐**  Rough Task Ideas — 5 \- 8 or more tasks, each mapped to a workflow on the approved [Task Selection tracker.](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1YRUwLm3oLjlL2v2g-_lw9rC_NeJ5gcpHBX6_M_HHh4c/edit?gid=668143205#gid=668143205) At least one P0.

| Self-check before submitting |
| :---- |

**☐**  Setting/specialty is named explicitly ("inpatient hospital medicine," not just "hospital").

**☐**  Frictions are about people, not information gaps (info gaps are traps).

**☐**  Each trap requires synthesis across 2+ documents — not solvable from one file.

**☐**  At least 3 trap types represented (copy-forward, buried finding, source-of-truth, temporal, SDOH, admin error).

**☐**  At least one task is P0 priority and labelled as such.

**☐**  Each task names a concrete deliverable — not an open-ended question.

**☐**  Self-containment risks acknowledged (anything the task needs that might not be in the chart).

| Do / Don't |  |
| :---- | :---- |
| **DO** | **DON'T** |
| **✓**  Start with YOUR clinical pain points — "the cases that drive me up the wall." | **✗**  Start with a textbook diagnosis or a zebra. "This patient has 5 rare conditions" creates fake complexity. **✗**  Stack rare diseases. Real complexity is HFrEF \+ pAF \+ CKD \+ COPD \+ DM \+ obesity, not 5 zebras. |
| **✓**  Aim for multiple comorbidities, long medication lists. Complexity from common conditions intersecting. | **✗** Use a patient case who is a 25 year old male with an unremarkable past medical and surgical history and only takes Zyrtec for allergies.   |
| **✓**  Include 2+ real frictions — specialist vs specialist, family vs team, PCP vs admitting. | **✗**  Confuse frictions with traps. Specialist disagreement \= friction. Buried lab finding \= trap |
| **✓**  Make sure you have both world-level and task-level traps that are” reasonably ambiguous” but still fair game | **✗**  Have traps that are glaringly obvious that the model will immediately pick up on them  |
| **✓**  Map every task to a P0/P1/P2 workflow on the approved tracker. At least one P0. | **✗**  Invent a workflow. If your task doesn't fit, ask in Slack. |
