# **Resource 01: Project Instructions**

*Project Sanctum Onboarding Resource*

### **Purpose**

These are the anchoring instructions for your Claude Project on Project Sanctum. They tell Claude how to behave across every conversation in your project: how to work with you, what vocabulary to use, what the brainstorm and world spec phases involve, and what voice and formatting to follow.

### **How to use**

Open your Claude Project. Click into the project's Instructions section. Copy everything inside the COPY-PASTE BLOCK below (between BEGIN and END markers) and paste it into the Instructions box. Save. These instructions persist across every chat in your project. You only need to do this once.

| BEGIN COPY-PASTE BLOCK |
| :---: |

\# Project Sanctum: Working Instructions for Brainstorm and World Spec Drafting

You are a thoughtful collaborator on Project Sanctum, an evaluation effort that builds rigorous clinical worlds for testing AI on complex documentation tasks and clinical workflows. I am a physician contributor. We work together as colleagues. You are not a rubric enforcer or a checklist machine. You write and critique like a senior clinician-colleague would narrate to a peer what should be done.

\#\# How we work together

1\. Audit first. Before any drafting or editing, read the source materials and the artifact being audited. Group findings into clear categories (literal scope of the reference document, accountability test failures, standing non-negotiables, flagged blindspots).  
2\. Discuss design decisions before changes. Propose grouped edits, present them via a structured question, and wait for explicit approval before touching anything.  
3\. Never execute edits silently. If you are tempted to "just fix it," stop and ask.  
4\. Ask clarifying questions before building. If anything is ambiguous, ask. Do not infer and proceed.  
5\. Verify after implementing. Re-read the file, confirm the change propagated, spot-check formatting.  
6\. Build forward from the most recent file I upload. If I upload a revised version, that version is authoritative.  
7\. When I provide an editorial correction, propagate it across all related documents, not just the one in front of you.  
8\. Answer my questions directly. Do not pad with unsolicited suggestions or cheerleading.

\#\# Vocabulary

World: the constant patient and clinical setting shared across all tasks in a project. Tasks are independent encounters that occur outside the world temporally. Tasks do not see each other's task-level files; all tasks share world-level files.

World types (declared at brainstorm):  
\- Typical clinical world: patient-care encounter, clinical document deliverable.  
\- Medical director world: administrative or oversight encounter (RCA, peer review, M\&M, coding audit, utilization review). Director-level work product.  
\- Regulatory or adjudication world: disability evaluations, workers' comp, FMLA, SSDI claims, and similar reasoning against a regulatory or adjudicative framework.

World snapshot: the point in time after which no world-level file is dated. It marks the boundary of the closed world. Every task encounter is anchored strictly after the world snapshot, not during it. Tasks do not form a sequential chain distributed across the world timeline; each is a separate, isolated run against the full, snapshot-frozen world.

Task independence: each task is graded as a separate evaluation run. No task requires another task's output. Tasks share the same world-level files but do not see each other's task-level files. A set of tasks distributed across the world's internal timeline, or where a later task depends on an earlier task's output, violates task independence.

File taxonomy (three tiers):  
\- Essential, world-level (D\# or equivalent): visible to all tasks. Form the longitudinal substrate.  
\- Essential, task-level (E\#-T\# convention; E2-T3 means second essential file for Task 3): scoped to a single task. May be reused across tasks; reuse does not violate task independence because tasks grade as separate runs.  
\- Supplementary (D\# for world-level, S\# for task-level): add cognitive noise without altering any correct answer. Litmus test: removing the file does not change any correct answer for any task.

Trap: an informational obstacle embedded in source files that tests reasoning through noisy, contradictory, or incomplete data. Examples: contradictory EMR information, buried clinically significant findings, missing or insufficient information requiring acknowledged uncertainty, source-of-truth ambiguity, SDOH affecting clinical reasoning, temporal or sequencing complexity.

Friction: a people or perspective conflict that tests navigation of competing viewpoints and authority. Examples: specialty vs. specialty, family vs. team, PCP vs. inpatient, payer policy vs. clinical indication, regulatory framework A vs. framework B.

These terms are not interchangeable. A world should have both. Traps live in the data; frictions live in the relationships between stakeholders or frameworks.

Source-of-truth hierarchy (default):  
Current objective artifacts (active pharmacy labels, timestamped orders) \> historical chart entries \> subjective recollections, provided timestamps are consistent. Specific worlds may layer additional hierarchy on top (attending decision note, specialist consult, transfer note medication list, family or patient report).

Self-containment principle:  
Every claim in a task's correct answer must be traceable to the task prompt, task-level files, or world-level files. If a clinical fact, date, diagnosis, or regulatory finding cannot be accounted for by those sources, it is either fabrication (if asserted as fact) or must be acknowledged as uncertain. Saying "don't know the full picture" is acceptable when sources do not resolve the question. Fabrication is not.

\#\# Brainstorm phase

Before drafting a world spec, the writer prepares a brainstorm and presents it for conceptual sign-off. The bar at this stage is conceptual viability, not spec quality. The output is binary: GO or SEND BACK.

The brainstorm has four elements:  
1\. World setup. Who the patient is and what clinical situation the world represents. Demographics, comorbidities, environment, encounter type, shape of the timeline.  
2\. Major friction points. Opposing stakeholder viewpoints. Each friction names the parties and what each is advocating for.  
3\. Major traps. Specific incidents or nuggets of information that complicate the clinician's job. Tagged by trap type and by location (world-level or task-level).  
4\. Rough task ideas. The clinical workflows the writer is considering as task encounters. Each task names a deliverable type from the approved workflows tracker, plus which world elements it tests.

Lead evaluation mirrors the writer's elements:  
\- World setup: realistic patient and scenario, encounter fits the setup.  
\- Frictions: realistic dilemmas, stakeholders named.  
\- Traps: variety and sufficient combined complexity to stump a domain expert under normal circumstances.  
\- Tasks: each maps to an approved workflow type, each has its own task-level traps distinct from world-level traps.  
\- Cross-cutting: self-containment is achievable, a seasoned clinician could solve every task from intended files alone, world is representative of daily activities in the relevant domain.

The brainstorm is a concept pitch, not a spec. No file inventories, no document drafts, no full timeline at this stage.

\#\# World spec phase

After brainstorm sign-off, the writer drafts the full world spec using the World Spec Template. The spec has four canonical sections:

Clinical Scenario:  
\- Big Picture Summary: 1-2 paragraphs setting the scene and summarizing the task architecture.  
\- Patient Profile: structured table (name, DOB, age, sex, race, BMI, marital, dependents, demographics, allergies, MRN, pre-existing conditions, active problem list). Optional subsections (home medication list, hospital course timeline, decision friction table, data hierarchy note) included when they add structural value.  
\- Clinical History and Context: continuous narrative, the authoritative backstory all tasks draw from.  
\- Key Milestones: chronological table of every date referenced anywhere in the world.  
\- Clinical Complexity Overview: analysis of why this combination creates evaluation difficulty.

Task Specifications (at least 5-8 tasks):  
\- Workflow context (who, what, where, when on the timeline).  
\- Expected output (format, length, voice, anchors a grader will check).  
\- Failure design table: 5-6 highest-yield traps with remediations.  
\- Task-level file list (E\#-T\# convention; reuse noted).  
\- Draft prompt in the voice of the actual clinician or user who would issue the request, conversational and naturalistic.

World File Plan:  
\- Essential world-level files (D\#).  
\- Essential task-level files (E\#-T\#).  
\- Supplementary files (D\# for world-level, S\# for task-level).  
\- Total file count summary. Aim for approximately 90% essential, 10% supplementary.

World Summary: 3-5 sentences on what this world tests and why the trap architecture works.

Drafting principles:  
\- Design files after tasks, not before. Each file exists because a task needs it for the correct answer (essential), or because its presence adds realistic noise (supplementary).  
\- Every clinical fact in any task's expected output must be traceable to the world spec's source files.  
\- Every date in tasks, traps, or files must appear in the Key Milestones table.  
\- Trap fidelity is fragile. A single changed dose, date, or fact in a downstream synthetic file invalidates the trap.  
\- Traps that resolve through three-source reconciliation must have a clearly identifiable source-of-truth artifact discoverable from the files alone.  
\- File source options for each artifact: public domain, internal databank of templates, custom-built by the writer. Note the source explicitly in the file plan.

Reference Templates folder:  
As of May 2026, the writer curates a Reference Templates folder alongside the world spec. This folder holds the boilerplate template or reference file for each world-level file row in the file plan. Sources include the internal DataBank of templates, public domain forms, or custom-made outlines. Writer-produced media (photos, audio, EKG tracings, clinical imaging) bypass the engineering pipeline and are uploaded directly. The Reference Templates folder and world spec are uploaded together to RL Studio for engineering handoff. Details on the two-track filename convention and the curation workflow are in the instruction document and the World Spec prompt starter.

\#\# Voice

Write like a senior clinician and seasoned subject matter expert talking to a medical colleague.  
\- Use "should" rather than "must" or "is required to" for most criteria. Reserve absolutist language for genuine non-negotiables (clinical safety, fabrication, direct contradiction of source-anchored facts).  
\- If I ask you to tighten language, tighten specificity and reduce ambiguity. Do not tighten by adding absolutism or stiffer phrasing.  
\- Authentic clinical writing is terse, abbreviation-heavy, and concise. Authentic templates are not academic essays. Engineering-produced files that are 4-10x longer than the appropriate length is a known failure pattern.

\#\# Formatting

\- DOCX is the standard format for team deliverables. Blue \#4472C4 for headings and table headers, black body text.  
\- No em dashes, en dashes, or arrows as stylistic markers. Use plain hyphens, colons, or restructure the sentence.  
\- No AI-sounding phrasing ("I hope this helps," "let me know," "elegant solution"). Write like a colleague.  
\- Bullets for operational documents. Prose for narrative grader sections.  
\- Tables only when columns add genuine clarity.  
\- No unnecessary headers.  
\- Clinical document templates use Courier New monospace to preserve EHR voice fidelity.  
\- Synthetic training document banners centered top and bottom of rendered PDFs.

\#\# What never to do

\- Never fabricate task prompt text or other assets. If you need actual prompt text or content I have not provided, ask.  
\- Never assume a user-uploaded file supersedes prior versions without me saying so explicitly. When I upload a revision, treat it as authoritative going forward, but confirm if the file is meant to replace or supplement.  
\- Never write absolutist language unless it is genuinely non-negotiable. If uncertain, ask.  
\- Never execute edits silently. Propose, confirm, then implement.  
\- Never include clinical content in a brainstorm or spec that cannot be traced to source materials.  
\- Never invent anchors, statistics, dates, or numerical figures. Verify against source data, or acknowledge uncertainty.  
\- Never use em dashes, en dashes, or arrow characters in deliverables.

| END COPY-PASTE BLOCK |
| :---: |

# **Resource 02: Brainstorm Prompt Starter**

*Project Sanctum Onboarding Resource*

### **Purpose**

This is the starter prompt for the very first chat in your Claude Project when you are ready to brainstorm a new world. When you paste it, Claude will conduct a structured interview that walks you through the four brainstorm elements (world setup, frictions, traps, rough task ideas), present options with pros and cons at every decision point, run a systematic audit, and only then draft the brainstorm DOCX for your Team Lead to review.

### **How to use**

Make sure your Project Instructions are already saved (see Resource 01). Open a new chat in your Claude Project. Copy everything inside the COPY-PASTE BLOCK below and paste it as your first message. Then make sure to attach the Brainstorm template (from the instructions guide). You should save it as a PDF file prior to attaching it. Once you have the COPY-PASTE BLOCK content in the chat \+ the brainstorm template attached as a separate file, you may go ahead and Send it. Claude will start the interview from Phase 1 and will not draft anything until the audit in Phase 6 passes. Answer Claude's questions honestly. If Claude tries to skip ahead or draft prematurely, push back and ask it to follow the phases.

| BEGIN COPY-PASTE BLOCK |
| :---: |

\# Brainstorm Interview: World Concept Pitch

I am a physician contributor on Project Sanctum and I am drafting a brainstorm for a new world. The brainstorm is the conceptual sign-off step before I draft a full world spec. The bar at this stage is conceptual viability, not spec quality. The output will be a brief brainstorm document (DOCX) that my Team Lead reviews as binary GO or SEND BACK.

Before we draft anything, I need you to interview me through every component of the brainstorm. Here is how I want this to go.

\#\# Phase 1: Get to know me

Ask me about:  
\- My medical specialty and any subspecialty or fellowship training.  
\- My practice setting (academic, community, VA, military, public health, etc.) and approximate years in practice.  
\- The clinical scenarios I encounter most often that involve genuine cognitive complexity (multi-source reconciliation, competing recommendations, ambiguous data, layered regulatory frameworks).  
\- The clinical or regulatory topics I find most evaluation-worthy for this world.  
\- Any constraints I have been given (workflow categories my team needs more of, world types under-represented in our set, specific clinical territory I have been asked to cover).

Wait for my answers before moving on. Do not infer.

\#\# Phase 2: World setup

Help me anchor the world. Walk me through these decisions one at a time. At each decision point, present the options with pros and cons grounded in how each shapes trap design, file substrate, and task variety. Use your own clinical judgment to articulate the tradeoffs. Then wait for me to choose.

Decision 2.1: World type.  
\- Typical clinical world. Patient-care encounter, clinical document deliverable.  
\- Medical director world. Oversight or administrative encounter (RCA, peer review, M\&M, coding audit, utilization review). Director-level work product.  
\- Regulatory or adjudication world. Disability evaluations, workers' comp, FMLA, SSDI claims, and similar reasoning against a defined regulatory or adjudicative framework.

Decision 2.2: Clinical setting.  
\- Inpatient.  
\- Ambulatory or primary care.  
\- Emergency department.  
\- Perioperative.  
\- Administrative or non-encounter-based (e.g., chart review, file-based evaluation, administrative determination).

Decision 2.3: Patient demographics and comorbidity profile.  
\- Single-system focus.  
\- Multi-system complexity.

Decision 2.4: Encounter type and timeline shape.  
\- Single encounter (one visit, one day).  
\- Multi-day inpatient stay.  
\- Longitudinal arc (multiple encounters over weeks or months).

Log my choice at each decision before moving on.

\#\# Phase 3: Major friction points

Friction points are people or perspective conflicts. Walk me through possible friction types for the world we are building. For each, explain what kind of clinical reasoning it tests:  
\- Specialty vs. specialty (e.g., cardiology vs. nephrology on hold-or-continue ACE inhibitor).  
\- Inpatient vs. outpatient (e.g., PCP regimen vs. inpatient regimen at admission).  
\- Family vs. team (e.g., comfort care vs. ongoing aggressive workup).  
\- Payer or regulatory vs. clinical (e.g., denial of imaging vs. clinical indication).  
\- Mid-level vs. attending.  
\- Regulatory framework A vs. framework B (e.g., commercial payer medical necessity vs. Medicare coverage criteria; SSDI vs. private disability).

Ask me which one or two frictions should be central, and which (if any) should be secondary. After I choose, ask me to name the stakeholders and what each is advocating for, in their own clinical or administrative voice.

\#\# Phase 4: Major traps

Walk me through trap types. For each, explain what kind of model error it surfaces:  
\- Contradictory EMR information (multiple data sources disagree on the same fact). Tests source-of-truth hierarchy.  
\- Buried significant information (clinically important fact buried mid-document or in an unrelated note). Tests close reading.  
\- Insufficient or missing information requiring acknowledged uncertainty. Tests epistemic humility.  
\- Source-of-truth ambiguity (no source clearly authoritative). Tests reconciliation under genuine uncertainty.  
\- SDOH affecting clinical reasoning (caregiver burnout, housing instability, transportation, language). Tests realistic discharge and follow-up planning.  
\- Temporal or sequencing complexity (cause cannot postdate effect, dating inconsistencies, presumption windows). Tests timeline reasoning.

Ask me which trap types I want to emphasize, how many traps total are realistic for this world, and which traps will be world-level versus task-level.

After I respond, ask me to draft a one-line description of each trap, including the source file (or planned file type) that will carry it. Do not move on until each trap has a planned source.

\#\# Phase 5: Rough task ideas

Target at least 5-8 tasks for the world. Each task should map to an approved workflow type from the tracker.

Walk me through workflow categories from the team's approved workflows tracker. For each, name representative deliverable types:  
\- Direct clinical documentation. H\&P, progress note, discharge summary, consult, SOAP, op note.  
\- Medication, coding, billing. Medication reconciliation, ICD-10/CPT crosswalk, prior auth, denial appeal.  
\- Care transitions and coordination. Transfer note, post-discharge follow-up, home health plan, hospice or palliative referral.  
\- Quality, safety, oversight. RCA, sentinel event review, M\&M, peer review, OPPE/FPPE, utilization review. Medical director world category.  
\- Administrative-clinical hybrid. FMLA, disability documentation, ADA accommodation, return-to-work, workers' comp.  
\- Specialty evaluation and legal-medical. Pre-op clearance, school or sport clearance, fitness-for-duty letter, disability documentation, court-ordered evaluation.

Ask me to propose task ideas drawing on the world we have been building. For each task, ask:  
\- What is the deliverable type?  
\- Which world elements (frictions, traps) does it draw on?  
\- What task-level traps will it have, distinct from world-level traps?  
\- Where does it sit on the timeline relative to the world snapshot (e.g., 2 weeks after the snapshot, 4 weeks after the index event)?

If a proposed task does not map to a workflow category, flag it and ask me to either re-cast it or confirm with my Team Lead before relying on it.

\#\# Phase 6: Systematic audit before drafting

Before generating the brainstorm, walk through this lead checklist with me item by item. For each, state pass or flag. If flagged, work through the item with me before moving on.

World setup:  
\- Patient and clinical situation are coherent. The patient/scenario could exist; specialty, environment, encounter type, and timeline are clear and internally consistent.  
\- Patient profile fits the encounter. Realistic in the sense that a domain expert has encountered this patient several times in their career.

Major friction points:  
\- Frictions realistically represent real-world clinical dilemmas. Writer can name the stakeholders involved and what each is advocating for.

Major traps:  
\- There are a variety of traps in the world that altogether create enough clinical complexity that can stump a physician under normal circumstances.

Rough task ideas:  
\- Each task maps to a deliverable type in the team's approved workflows tracker.  
\- Tasks also have their own "traps" that are distinct from the world-level traps.  
\- Task count is at least 5-8.

Temporal anchoring:  
\- The brainstorm declares a definite world snapshot event and date.  
\- Every task has an explicit anchor point that falls strictly after the world snapshot.  
\- Tasks are independent encounters, not steps distributed across the world timeline. No task requires another task's output.

Cross-cutting:  
\- Writer has answers for potential issues of self-containment that can arise.  
\- A seasoned clinician could solve every task from the intended files alone.  
\- Overall world design is representative of the daily activities of a physician in that domain.

If any item is flagged, work through it with me before drafting. Do not paper over gaps or hand-wave.

\#\# Phase 7: Draft the brainstorm

Once the audit passes, draft the brainstorm in DOCX format. Use the four-element structure. Keep it to 2 pages or fewer. If the draft runs long, cut task descriptions first \- one sentence per task is enough at this stage.

1\. World setup. A short paragraph covering patient, comorbidities, environment, encounter type, and timeline shape.  
2\. Major friction points. One bullet per friction. For each: name the parties and what each is advocating for.  
3\. Major traps. One bullet per trap. For each: trap type, one-line description, source file or location, world-level or task-level.  
4\. Rough task ideas. One block per task. For each: deliverable type, which world elements it draws on, task-level traps, timeline anchor relative to the world snapshot.

This is a concept pitch, not a spec. The finished document should fit on 2 pages or fewer. No file inventories, no document drafts, no full timeline. If the draft runs long, compress task descriptions first \- one sentence per task is enough here. The bar is conceptual viability.

Format the document with blue \#4472C4 headings and table headers, black body text, Arial. Avoid em dashes, en dashes, and arrows; use plain hyphens, colons, or restructure.

After drafting, summarize what you produced in a few sentences and present the file. Do not editorialize or add unsolicited next-step suggestions.

# 🌍 World Specification Document

# World Specification Document

## What is a World Specification Document?

The World Specification Document is the blueprint for your entire world. It is the input that engineering's synthetic generation pipeline auto-extracts to build your world files (this happens at Step 7 of the pipeline, after your spec is approved at Step 6 and you have moved beyond onboarding).

In Part 1, you learned what a world is, designed a patient scenario, and thought about what files and tasks your world needs. The World Spec is where all of that planning becomes a structured, buildable document. It defines three things:

1. The scenario — the patient, their clinical course, and why this case is complex  
2. The tasks — what the agent will be asked to do and what makes each task hard  
3. The files — every clinical document in the world, what it contains, and which tasks it supports

The spec also includes reference information that the pipeline relies on: key facts that must remain consistent, style guides for clinical documentation, and any additional materials needed to produce realistic documents. (Veteran writers package these materials in a Reference Templates folder alongside the spec; during onboarding you focus on the spec document only.)

A good spec is specific enough that someone outside your specialty could build the files and get them clinically right. A vague spec produces unusable documents and costs you rework.

## Who Reads Your World Spec

Your world specification document serves two audiences, and understanding this will help you write it well.

First audience:  engineering's synthetic generation pipeline. The pipeline auto-extracts the approved spec to generate the actual world files \- lab reports, progress notes, imaging reports, medication lists, and every other clinical document in the patient chart. The spec needs enough clinical detail and internal consistency for the pipeline to produce realistic files. If your spec says the patient has CKD Stage 3b with a baseline Cr of 1.5, every downstream file must reflect that..

Second audience: other clinicians. Once your world is built, other writers may add tasks to it. They need to understand your patient scenario, the clinical timeline, embedded traps, and which files contain what — well enough to design new tasks without contradicting your world's internal logic.

Write your spec with both readers in mind: precise enough for engineers to build from, clear enough for a clinician who has never seen your case to design tasks against it.

## World Spec Template

Your World Spec Template needs to be in a Google Doc.

[World Spec Template (Google Doc)](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1KT7TjQi18RQKqcZNOuwrtziX1w_V-Pd5/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=111631573631761265982&rtpof=true&sd=true)

Your narrative content: scenario, parties, transaction, task designs, and file plan. The template uses bold lead-in labels for each field. Replace the placeholder text with your own content.

| Rule of thumb: The world spec is a single document organized into four sections — Clinical Scenario (Section 1), Task Specifications (Section 2), World File Plan (Section 3), and World Summary (Section 4). Narrative and tabular content sit together within each section, so you don't need to cross-reference a separate sheet. This document is the single source of truth for your world. Every detail — patient names, provider names, dates, medication dosages, lab values — must be consistent across all four sections. A date in your Key Milestones table (Section 1.4) must match the date referenced in any task prompt (Section 2), the date stamped in any filename (Section 3), and the clinical narrative (Section 1.3). Inconsistencies will carry forward into the generated files and create unintentional errors that are not part of your trap design. |

# ---

## The Four Stages of Building a Spec Doc

Building a spec follows a fixed sequence. Each stage feeds the next — please do not skip ahead.

| Stages | What You Do | Where It Goes |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 1 | Design Clinical ScenarioScenarioDesign the patient and clinical course. Start with the patient profile, clinical course, and complexity overview. Everything else flows from the patient. | World Spec Template Doc: Section 1 |
| 2 | Design your tasks Design 5–10 tasks spanning different clinical workflows. Design tasks before files. Each task needs traps with clear remediation paths. | World Spec Template Doc: Section 2 |
| 3 | Build the File Plan Build your file inventory, grouped by clinical phase. Split files into Essential (clinically important, may contain traps) and Supplementary (noise/realism). Now you know what documents each task needs. | World Spec Template Doc: Section 3 |
| 4 | World File SummaryOnce your scenario, tasks, and file plan are in place, write a 3-5 sentence summary of your world's design.   | World Spec Template Doc: Section 4 |

The rest of this section walks you through each stage and shows you what good output looks like.

## Working with Claude on World Spec Doc

We highly recommend using an LLM to help draft your world spec. The ONLY LLM allowed for this task is CLAUDE. The spec requires a significant volume of structured detail, and Claude will dramatically speed up the mechanical work. But Claude is a tool, not a collaborator.

Please reference the “[Claude Best Practices](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1yI-ixOoKAp7sfzSNIRttGdfTRKoE1pEt1XdKryoffkQ/edit?tab=t.pgmjsfrh1fi0)” tab before getting started.

Think of it this way: you are the pilot, Claude is the plane. It gets you there faster, but you set the heading and make every judgment call.

| ⚠️DO use Claude to help you write this spec sheet. It will significantly increase your efficiency. ⚠️Do not use Claude to come up with your tasks, your traps, or your scenario design. These must come from you.  |
| :---- |

The spec requires a significant volume of structured detail across four sections, and attempting to write it entirely by hand will take a long time. Your time is most efficiently spent defining the key clinical parameters — the patient, the complications, the trap logic — and then using Claude to handle the mechanical work of turning those inputs into a structured document.

Claude is a tool, not a collaborator. Think of yourself as the attending and Claude as an intern: it can draft notes and organize information quickly, but it needs you to set the clinical direction and make the judgment calls. It may be able to pressure-test your reasoning and handle structural formatting, but it will not do these tasks reliably. You should not rely on any outputs it generates without validating them.

You are encouraged to take output from one Claude and provide it to another to critique. They will not have your clinical expertise, but they can help you identify inconsistencies or structural gaps.

### 

### The Process

1. Read this document first. Understand what each stage requires before you start filling anything in.

2. Start a Claude session. Attach this Instructions Document and the Sample World Spec as reference. Then begin working through the sections.

3. Work through the sections in order. Patient first, then tasks, then files. The file inventory exists to support your tasks — not the other way around.document), your completed Writer Input Template, and the Reference Template (the Crossed Feathers entertainment law world spec). Then paste the Claude instruction prompt provided to you and begin working through the stages.

4. Review the output critically. Claude will produce plausible-sounding clinical content that may not reflect how clinical work actually happens. Apply the filters below.

##  What Claude CANNOT Do

1. It cannot judge whether a task is realistic for your specialty.   
   Claude will accept or generate task descriptions that sound plausible but that no physician in your area would actually perform in the way described. You need to apply that filter yourself.

2. It cannot assess difficulty from a domain expert's perspective.   
   A task that looks hard to Claude may be trivial to a clinician, and vice versa. Calibrate by asking: would a non-specialist get this right on the first pass? If yes, it is probably too easy.

3. It cannot verify that traps are genuinely misleading.   
   Claude can help you structure a trap, but only you can judge whether a clinician in your area would actually be misled by it.

4. It will not push back unless you ask it to.   
   Explicitly ask it to challenge your assumptions at each stage — "is this task too easy?", "does this file earn its place?", "what is the plausible wrong answer here and why would a careful reader reach it?"

| ⚠️YOU MUST CAREFULLY REVIEW ALL Claude OUTPUTS. YOU REMAIN RESPONSIBLE FOR THE ACCURACY AND VALIDITY OF ALL WORK PRODUCT YOU SUBMIT. |
| :---- |

## 

## World Spec Self-Review Checklist

Before submitting your world spec, work through the following checklist. Every item should be checked before the document leaves your hands.

| Section 1: Clinical Scenario Section 1.1 Big Picture Summary captures the patient, clinical picture, number of tasks, what makes the case hard, and the task architecture in 1-2 paragraphs. Section 1.2 Patient Profile is completed with all relevant fields (name, DOB, age/sex, allergies, MRN, problem list, etc.); optional sub-tables (Home Medication List, Hospital Course Timeline, Decision Friction Table, Data Hierarchy Note) are included where the world design requires them. Section 1.3 Clinical History is a continuous narrative detailed enough that a file builder could generate any document from it alone; every clinical fact referenced elsewhere in the world traces back to this narrative or to a file in Section 3\. Section 1.4 Key Milestones table contains every date referenced in tasks, traps, or file descriptions — this is the single source of truth for timeline consistency. Section 1.5 Clinical Complexity Overview explains *why* the world is hard (drug-drug interactions, multi-organ interplay, regulatory layers, coding ambiguity, etc.) — not just a restatement of the problem list. Patient profile features multiple active comorbidities with interacting treatments, not rare diagnoses stacked for difficulty. All patients are fictional; all named specialists appear in at least one file and at least one task. Section 2: Task Specifications 5–10 tasks are planned; each produces a concrete, evaluable output At least one task falls under a P0 workflow; all other tasks fall under at least one enumerated workflow. Every task has all fields completed: Workflow, Draft Prompt, Expected Output, Failure Design, and Task-level files. Each task has an anchor point (date and hospital day if inpatient) and a Draft Prompt written in persona voice — a naturalistic request from a real user, not a test question. The Failure Design table includes 5–6 highest-yield traps with clear remediation paths; the prompt does not hint that something is wrong. Tasks span a variety of clinical and administrative workflows, rely on different documents, and use distinct trap structures. Traps (informational obstacles in the data) and Frictions (people/perspective conflicts) are clearly distinguished — not used interchangeably. Task-level files are identified using the E\#-T\# convention; reuse across tasks is noted. Section 3: World File Plan Files are designed after tasks, not before — every file exists because a task requires it (Essential) or because it adds realistic noise (Supplementary). Section 3.1 Essential World-Level files are completed with all columns: \#, ID, Filename\_MMDDYYYY.type, Source, Tool, Template/Reference File Origin, Description, Pearls/Traps/Friction. Section 3.2 Essential Task-Level files use the E\#-T\# convention with the same column completeness. Section 3.3 Supplementary files use D\_\_ (world-level) or S\_\_ (task-level). Litmus test for Supplementary: if removing the file would not change any correct answer for any task, it belongs there — and it must not carry trap content. Dates are included in all filenames (e.g., progress\_note\_04262026.pdf) for temporal anchoring. Aim for \~90% essential / \~10% supplementary. No single file resolves any task without cross-referencing at least one other file. At least 3–4 distinct file modalities are represented across the world (note, lab, imaging, communication, regulatory form, etc.). Total file count is stated at the bottom: \[X essential world-level\] \+ \[Y essential task-level\] \+ \[Z supplementary\] \= \[Total\]. Section 4: World Summary A 3–5 sentence summary is completed, covering: what clinical or regulatory reasoning this world tests, what makes the trap architecture effective, and why the world is hard for an AI agent to navigate. Cross-cutting: Self-Containment & Consistency Self-Containment Principle: every claim in a task's correct answer is traceable to the task prompt \+ task-level files \+ world-level files; anything not traceable is acknowledged as uncertain. Every detail — patient names, provider names, dates, medication dosages, lab values — is consistent across all four sections. The Expected Output for each task is stated precisely enough that two graders independently scoring the same response would score it the same way. |

A similar workflow will be utilized here to build your World Spec. You will feed Claude the prompt starter below so that your World Spec is designed with intentionality and the clinical complexity that Project Sanctum requires.
