# **Resource 03: World Spec Prompt Starter**

*Project Sanctum Onboarding Resource*

**Purpose**

This is the starter prompt for the chat in which you draft your full world spec. It assumes your brainstorm has been signed off by your Team Lead. When you paste it, Claude will load your approved brainstorm, then walk you through every section of the World Spec Template (Clinical Scenario, Task Specifications, World File Plan, World Summary), present clinical-trajectory options with pros and cons at every decision point, run a systematic audit, and only then draft the spec DOCX.

**How to use**

Have your approved brainstorm ready (DOCX or pasted text). Open a new chat in your Claude Project (a fresh chat is recommended so the world spec session is self-contained). Copy everything inside the COPY-PASTE BLOCK below and paste it as your first message. Send it. Claude will ask for your brainstorm in Phase 1 and walk through every section before drafting in Phase 7\.

**BEGIN COPY-PASTE BLOCK**

\# World Spec Interview: Full Specification Drafting

I am a physician contributor on Project Sanctum and my world brainstorm has been signed off by my Pod Lead (or assigned reviewer). I am now ready to draft the full world spec using the World Spec Template. Before we draft anything, I need you to interview me through every component of the template. By the way, I will also need to upload the Excel Sheet that contains the approved task selection categories (i.e. clinical workflows, healthcare deliverables, etc.) for Project Sanctum so that the tasks I end up designing are aligned to project expectations. Here is how I want this to go.

\#\# Phase 1: Load the brainstorm

Ask me to share my approved brainstorm now. I will paste it in the chat or upload the DOCX. Once I share it, summarize back in your own words what you understand:

\- World type (typical clinical, medical director, or regulatory/adjudication).  
\- Setting and timeline shape.  
\- Patient sketch.  
\- Frictions, with stakeholders.  
\- Traps, by type and location (world-level vs. task-level).  
\- Task list, with deliverable type and timeline placement.

Confirm with me before proceeding. If anything is unclear or missing, ask.

\#\# Phase 2: Clinical Scenario

Walk me through each subsection. Ask focused questions, present options where there are real design choices, and explain the pros and cons.

\#\#\# Big Picture Summary

Per the World Spec Template, this subsection is 1-2 paragraphs that set the scene and summarize the task architecture. Walk me through it in two parts.

Paragraph 1 \- Setting the scene. Ask me:  
\- What type of patient is presenting?  
\- What is the clinical picture?  
\- What makes this case hard?

Lead with the patient and the problem, not the institution or setting.

Paragraph 2 \- Task architecture and file set composition. Ask me:  
\- How many tasks total? (Target at least 5-8.)  
\- What are the tasks representing in terms of clinical workflow or workflows?  
\- What do the tasks aim to highlight in terms of pain points faced by a physician?  
\- High-level world file set composition (e.g., "21 essential world-level files, 3 supplementary, 15 task-level"). We will refine the exact count in the World File Plan section, but a working estimate goes here.

Draft the subsection after I respond, then read it back for confirmation.

\#\#\# Patient Profile

Walk me through each row of the profile table. For each, ask the question. Default to omitting a row when it does not add clinical value.  
\- Name (fictional), DOB, age, sex.  
\- Race or ethnicity. Include only if clinically relevant. Ask whether it is.  
\- BMI. Include only if relevant.  
\- Marital status, dependents. Include if relevant to compensation, decision-making, or social context. Otherwise skip.  
\- Additional demographics. Occupation, SDOH. Ask whether these matter for the world's traps and tasks.  
\- Allergies (drug allergies with reaction type) and MRN (fictional).  
\- Pre-existing conditions. Conditions already established or adjudicated that the model must incorporate rather than re-derive. Ask me to list these.  
\- Active problem list. Complete list with relevant qualifiers (laterality, severity, treatment status, key dates).

Then ask whether to include any optional subsections. Each is described in the World Spec Template; surface them as available options and ask whether they add structural value to this world:  
\- Home medication list.  
\- Hospital course timeline.  
\- Decision friction table.  
\- Data hierarchy note.

\#\#\# Clinical History and Context

Ask me to narrate the clinical backstory in chronological order. This is the authoritative backstory all tasks draw from. Prompt me for:  
\- How the patient arrived at this point.  
\- Chronological progression of relevant conditions.  
\- Key diagnostic workups and their results.  
\- Surgical history.  
\- Transitions of care.  
\- Current clinical status at the world snapshot date.

For regulatory or adjudication worlds, also prompt for:  
\- Prior claims, adjudications, appeals.  
\- Service or employment records.  
\- The specific regulatory framework the tasks reason against (e.g., the relevant statutory framework, agency rules, or coverage criteria).

After I narrate, draft the subsection and confirm. Every clinical fact mentioned anywhere else in the spec must be traceable here or to a source file in the World File Plan.

\#\#\# Key Milestones (Compressed Timeline)

Ask me for every date that will appear anywhere in tasks, traps, or files. Build a chronological table. For each date, capture the event and what trap or task it anchors. This table is the single source of truth for timeline consistency.

After I list dates, ask: are there any dates referenced in the brainstorm or in clinical history that I have not captured here? Flag any date in a task or trap that does not appear in this table. Do not let those dates float.

\#\#\# Clinical Complexity Overview

Ask me to articulate why this world is hard. Not a restatement of the problem list. An analysis of why the combination of conditions, data, and context creates evaluation difficulty. Prompt for:  
\- Drug-drug interactions, multi-organ interplay, competing treatment goals.  
\- Domain-specific complexity (regulatory layers, legal standards, coding ambiguity) where applicable.

A reader finishing this subsection should understand why an AI model would struggle with these tasks.

\#\# Phase 3: Task Specifications

NOTE: It is a NON-NEGOTIABLE for the writer (i.e. me) to personally come up with the task prompts. Our project prohibits the LLM (i.e. Claude) from coming up with the task prompt. The writer MUST produce the task prompts themselves, even if they are not 100% finalized.

Brainstorming is fine. But the actual written task prompt has to come from the writer. Once again, this is a non-negotiable.

For each task in the brainstorm, walk me through the structure below. Repeat this loop for every task. Do not batch-draft all tasks before confirming each.

\#\#\# Task title

Ask me for a short title that names the deliverable type and the specific scenario.

\#\#\# Workflow

Ask:  
\- Who is doing the work (role, training level)?  
\- What is happening (the encounter or task moment)?  
\- When is it happening relative to the world timeline?  
\- Where is it happening (clinic, ED, ward, telehealth, administrative setting)?

\#\#\# Expected output

Ask:  
\- Format (chart note, letter, structured form, table, narrative).  
\- Length band.  
\- Voice and style.  
\- Specific clinical content that constitutes a correct response.  
\- Key anchors a grader will check (specific medications, doses, dates, codes, ratings, findings).

This is the basis for the eventual golden response. Be specific about what correct looks like without writing the full golden here.

\#\#\# Failure design

Walk me through the 5 to 6 highest-yield traps for this task. For each, ask:  
\- What misleads the model? (the trap itself)  
\- How does a correct response handle this? (the remediation)

Distinguish task-level traps from world-level traps that this task happens to surface. Both belong in the table; tag each.

\#\#\# Task-level files

Ask which files are scoped to this task only (E\#-T\# convention) versus reused from world-level (D\#) or shared across multiple tasks. If shared with another task, note the reuse.

A file qualifies as task-level essential only if it contains information required for that task's correct answer that does not exist in any world-level file.

\#\#\# Draft prompt

NOTE: I want to repeat that the actual task prompt has to come from the writer, not the LLM. Brainstorming is encouraged but you have to ask me specifically what I want to write (even if it is just in draft form) for my task prompts. This is a non-negotiable for this project and it ensures that there is still human expertise in the loop.

Ask me to dictate or draft the prompt in the voice of the actual clinician or user who would issue the request. Keep it conversational. Include:  
\- The clinical context they would naturally provide.  
\- The documents they would attach or reference.  
\- Any constraints they would mention.

Do not write it as a test question or a rubric. If I draft something stiff, push back and ask for naturalistic phrasing.

After all tasks are walked through, confirm the placement of each task on the world timeline relative to the world snapshot.

\#\# Phase 4: World File Plan

Design files after tasks, not before. Each file exists because a task needs it for the correct answer (essential), or because its presence adds realistic noise (supplementary). Aim for approximately 90% essential, 10% supplementary.

| *IMPORTANT: Below is the best practice and workflow for the template/reference file portions of our production pipeline as of May 20th, 2026\. Writer gets brainstorm approved Writer drafts world spec Writer drafts [World File plan tables](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1yI-ixOoKAp7sfzSNIRttGdfTRKoE1pEt1XdKryoffkQ/edit?tab=t.3mqyby119mmz) in World Spec and starts to curate the template files that correspond to each world-level file Writer can go use the following resources (i.e. reference file origin) for curating their template files: [Databank of templates](https://docs.google.com/document/d/13tOzO_0RdOXjPV8268oUErxzR0B3Ie_w/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.wi2f5090iruq) [Custom made templates](https://med-data-nine.vercel.app/) (i.e. your own outline for what a pre-op note would look like for your specialty) [Public domain template](http://chrome-extension://efaidnbmnnnibpcajpcglclefindmkaj/https://www.uscis.gov/sites/default/files/document/forms/i-693.pdf) (i.e. government forms that you don't need to recreate yourself) For world-level files that are not appropriate for the engineering team pipeline such as custom EKG/EEG/Ventilation tracings, real-world photos, clinical imaging, audio files, lab reports, recently published JAMA article, etc., the writer will still curate these [(using our clinical data generators](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1yI-ixOoKAp7sfzSNIRttGdfTRKoE1pEt1XdKryoffkQ/edit?tab=t.m2jym6vilrev)*, *Nano Banana Pro, ElevenLabs, GarageBand, Photoshop, etc.) alongside the boilerplate template/reference files from the Databank, public domain, etc. ![:warning:][image18]Note: ALL  of these files will be uploaded to RL Studio for engineering handoff \--- engineering team will know exactly which ones are templates that they need to convert into actual synthetic files VS. which world-level files already finalized/created by the writer. Writer finalizes their selection of all world-level files including templates/reference files and custom-made files ![:warning:][image19]Note: While not required, we highly recommend you [organize your files in a Google Drive folder](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1yI-ixOoKAp7sfzSNIRttGdfTRKoE1pEt1XdKryoffkQ/edit?tab=t.kljloydyze2j) (using Mercor expert email) so that it is easier for you to upload and share if needed to reviewers. It is just best practice to have your own personal copies of your project materials organized in a user-friendly repository. Writer [self-QCs](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1yI-ixOoKAp7sfzSNIRttGdfTRKoE1pEt1XdKryoffkQ/edit?tab=t.7nvfbiksj92u) their finalized world spec and curated world-level template selection (+custom made world-level files) Writer goes to [RL Studio and uploads](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1yI-ixOoKAp7sfzSNIRttGdfTRKoE1pEt1XdKryoffkQ/edit?tab=t.ia89kuwlt2wz) world spec \+ world-level template selection (+custom made world-level files)*  |
| :---- |

\#\#\# Essential files (world-level)

Ask me to list every file that should be visible to all tasks. For each file, capture:  
\- ID (D1, D2, etc.).  
\- Filename with date suffix (Filename\_MMDDYYYY.type).  
\- Source. Three options per the World Spec Template: public domain, internal databank of templates, or custom-built by the writer.  
\- Description. What clinical content it contains, what content it does not contain, formatting expectations.  
\- Pearls and traps. The function for the patient, what a physician should learn from reading it, what traps are present, what frictions are surfaced.

A complex world may have 15 to 25 world-level essential files. Flag if the count is unusually low or high.

NOTE (for new writers): As of May 20th 2026, you curate a Reference Templates folder alongside the world spec. The file names you list here will be the FINAL synthetic filenames engineering produces. The template files you place in the Reference Templates folder use generic descriptive names (no datestamps). Writer-produced media (Nano Banana Pro, ElevenLabs, real-world photos, custom EKG/EEG tracings, clinical imaging, audio) bypass the engineering pipeline and are uploaded directly. All files are uploaded to RL Studio for engineering handoff.

\#\#\# Essential files (task-level)

Ask which files are scoped to specific tasks only. Use E\#-T\# convention (E1-T3 means first essential file for Task 3). For each file, capture the same fields plus the task it serves. If reused across tasks, note all serving tasks.

A file qualifies as task-level essential only if it contains information required for that task's correct answer that does not exist in any world-level file. If the information is in a world-level file already, it is not task-level essential.

\#\#\# Supplementary files

Ask which files add realistic noise without altering any task's correct answer. Apply the litmus test: removing this file does not change any correct answer for any task. Use D\# for world-level supplementary and S\# for task-level supplementary.

Capture the same fields. Confirm the litmus test for each before adding.

\#\#\# File count summary

Tally the totals. Essential world-level \+ essential task-level \+ supplementary \= total unique files. Flag any imbalance (e.g., far more supplementary than essential, or no task-level essentials). Confirm the mix is approximately 90% essential, 10% supplementary.

\#\# Phase 5: World Summary

Ask me to articulate, in 3 to 5 sentences:  
\- What clinical or regulatory reasoning this world tests.  
\- What makes the trap architecture effective.  
\- What a reviewer should understand about why this world is hard.

This section is read by leads, reviewers, and graders to calibrate expectations quickly. Keep it dense and signal-rich.

\#\# Phase 6: Systematic audit before drafting

Before drafting, walk through these structural checks with me item by item. For each, state pass or flag. If flagged, work through the item with me before moving on.

Temporal anchoring:  
\- The world spec declares a definite world snapshot event and date.  
\- Every task has an explicit anchor point that falls strictly after the world snapshot.  
\- Tasks are independent encounters, not steps distributed across the world timeline. No task requires another task's output.

Self-containment and traceability:  
\- Every clinical fact in any task's expected output is traceable to the Clinical History narrative or a file in the World File Plan.  
\- Every date in tasks, traps, or files appears in the Key Milestones table.  
\- Every trap has an identifiable source file that carries it.

File plan integrity:  
\- Files were designed after tasks. Every essential file exists because a task needs it for the correct answer.  
\- Every supplementary file passes the litmus test: removing it does not change any correct answer for any task.  
\- Essential vs supplementary mix is approximately 90% essential, 10% supplementary.  
\- The file plan ID nomenclature is intentional and consistent: D\# for world-level, E\#-T\# for task-level essential, S\# or S\#-T\# for supplementary.

Cross-cutting:  
\- A seasoned clinician could solve every task from the intended files alone.  
\- The world is representative of the daily activities of a physician in the relevant domain.  
\- The task count is at least 5-8.

If any item is flagged, work through it with me before drafting. Do not paper over gaps or hand-wave. Wait for me to confirm before moving to Phase 7\.

\#\# Phase 7: Draft the world spec

Once I confirm we are ready, draft the spec in DOCX format using the World Spec Template structure:

1\. Clinical Scenario (Big Picture Summary, Patient Profile, Clinical History and Context, Key Milestones, Clinical Complexity Overview).  
2\. Task Specifications. One block per task: Workflow, Expected Output, Failure Design table, Task-Level Files, Draft Prompt.  
3\. World File Plan (Essential world-level, Essential task-level, Supplementary, file count summary).  
4\. World Summary.

Cover page should include world number, title, patient name (fictional), world type, setting, specialty/workflow, number of tasks, project name, and version.

Format the document with blue \#4472C4 headings and table headers, black body text, Arial. Avoid em dashes, en dashes, and arrows; use plain hyphens, colons, or restructure.

After drafting, summarize what you produced in a few sentences and present the file. Do not editorialize or add unsolicited next-step suggestions.

**END COPY-PASTE BLOCK**

# 🤖 FAQ: Claude

# **Troubleshooting and FAQ**

This section covers the most common issues writers encounter during the template and reference file workflow. If your question is not answered here, ask your pod lead or reviewer in Slack.

## **Claude Project and setup**

### **I cannot find "Projects" in Claude.**

Make sure you are signed in at claude.ai (not a different Claude interface). Projects is in the left sidebar. If you do not see it, your account may not have access. Ask your pod lead to confirm your account is set up correctly.

### **I do not know which email to use for Claude.**

Use your personal email. There is a known blocker for mercor.expert emails (SSO).

### **Claude says it cannot read one of my files.**

Confirm the file is a .docx (not .doc, .pdf, or .pages). If the file is very large, try re-saving it as a fresh .docx. If the problem persists, ask your pod lead.

## **Working with Claude**

### **Claude is producing everything at once instead of working in installments.**

The system prompt instructs Claude to work in installments. If Claude ignores this, paste the following reminder: "Please work in installments of 3 to 5 rows. Pause and check in with me after each batch before continuing."

### **Claude is going faster than I can keep up with.**

Tell Claude to pause. Example: "Pause. Let me review EW1 to EW3 before you continue. I will tell you when to proceed."

### **Claude asks a question I do not understand.**

Ask Claude to rephrase: "I do not understand your question. Can you rephrase it in simpler terms?" If it is still unclear, copy the question and paste it to your pod lead in Slack for help.

### **Claude produced a template that does not match what I had in mind.**

Tell Claude exactly which row and what to fix. Example: "For EW3, the template you produced is an inpatient progress note but my spec describes an outpatient clinic visit. Please redo EW3 using DB\_Progress\_Note\_Outpatient.docx instead." You do not have to start over; Claude can redo individual rows.

### **Claude seems to be making up content that is not in the DataBank.**

The system prompt tells Claude never to fabricate. If you suspect Claude is inventing a template rather than extracting from the DataBank, ask: "Is this template from the DataBank, or did you draft it from scratch? If you drafted it, which row in my spec required a custom-made template?" If the issue persists, flag it to your pod lead.

### **My Claude session timed out or got cut off in the middle of a batch.**

Start a new chat in the same Claude Project. Re-attach all three files and paste the prompt starter again. Then tell Claude where you left off: "We were working on my world-level files. You already completed EW1 through EW5. Please continue from WS1."

### **Claude is using em dashes, en dashes, or AI-sounding phrasing.**

Remind it: "Please do not use em dashes, en dashes, or AI-sounding phrasing in any template you produce. Use plain hyphens or restructure the sentence."

### **Claude produced a file I cannot open.**

Make sure you have Microsoft Word or Google Docs available. Claude produces .docx files. If the file appears corrupted, ask Claude to regenerate it: "The file for EW3 appears corrupted. Please regenerate it."

## **DataBank and templates**

### **The DataBank template I named does not exist.**

Open the DataBank and search for the template by keyword (not exact filename). You may have misspelled the filename in your spec. If no match exists, decide whether to use a different DataBank template, mark the row as custom-made, or ask your pod lead for guidance.

### **Two DataBank templates seem similar. Which one do I use?**

Open both templates and read through them. Pick the one that more closely matches the clinical document described in your spec row. If you are still unsure, ask your pod lead or reviewer.

### **The DataBank does not have a template for my specialty.**

Mark the row as custom-made in the Reference File Origin column. Claude can help you draft the template from scratch, or you can use the custom template generator as a starting point. If your specialty is frequently underrepresented, flag it to your pod lead so the DataBank can be updated for future writers.

### **A DataBank template looks outdated or has errors.**

Do not fix it yourself. Flag the specific template and the issue to your pod lead in Slack. Use the template as-is for now unless your pod lead tells you otherwise.

## **File naming**

### **The template filename does not match the Filename.type in my spec.**

That is correct and expected. The Filename.type column is the final synthetic filename engineering will produce (with a datestamp). The template filename is generic (no datestamp). Do not rename your templates. See Appendix B for the full explanation.

### **I do not know what to name my custom-made template.**

Use a descriptive name that makes it obvious what the document is. Follow the pattern: what it is \+ where it is from. Examples: HogwartsHospital\_Pre-OP\_Template.docx, CardiacRehab\_ProgressNote\_Template.docx. No datestamps on templates.

### **I do not know what to name my writer-produced file.**

Writer-produced files that will NOT go through engineering should use the final synthetic filename (WITH datestamp) from the Filename.type column in your spec. Example: HandwrittenMedList.05.15.2019.png.

### **I accidentally renamed a template to match the Filename.type column.**

Rename it back to the generic template name (no datestamp). If you are unsure what the original name was, check the Reference File Origin column in your spec or ask Claude to remind you.

## **Writer-produced files**

### **I am not sure if a file should be writer-produced or a template.**

Ask yourself: can an engineer who is not a physician produce a realistic version of this file from a template? If yes, it is a template for engineering. If it requires your clinical domain expertise, specialty knowledge, or a tool like Nano Banana Pro or ElevenLabs to create, it is writer-produced. If still unsure, ask your pod lead.

### **I do not know how to use Nano Banana Pro / ElevenLabs / the clinical data generators.**

Refer to the clinical data generators guide linked in Step 3\. If you need additional help with a specific tool, ask your pod lead or reviewer. They can walk you through it or point you to a tutorial.

### **I produced a file but I am not sure if it is good enough to submit.**

Open the file and ask: does this look like a realistic version of what it is supposed to represent? If it is a pill bottle photo, does it look like an actual pill bottle? If it is an EKG tracing, would a clinician recognize it as plausible? If you are unsure, share it with your pod lead or reviewer for a quick gut check before uploading.

### **Claude reminded me about writer-produced files I have not created yet.**

This is the system prompt working as intended. Claude tracks which rows are writer-produced and reminds you before you finish. Produce those files using the appropriate tools, add them to your folder, and include them when you upload to RL Studio.

## **World Spec and Reference File Origin**

### **I am confused about the Reference File Origin column.**

The Reference File Origin column tells Claude (and engineering) where each template comes from. For each row, you write one of: the DataBank template filename, Custom made (brief description), Public Domain (form name: source agency), or Writer-produced (brief description, tool). See Step 3 for examples of each.

### **I am not sure which origin to pick for a particular row.**

Start with the DataBank. Open it and search for a template that fits. If nothing fits, decide whether the document is a standard government form (public domain) or something you need to outline yourself (custom-made). If the file requires clinical expertise or specialty tools (photos, audio, tracings), mark it as writer-produced. When in doubt, ask your pod lead.

### **I am not sure if a row is world-level or task-level.**

World-level files are shared across all tasks in the world. Task-level files are specific to a single task. If the file would appear in every clinical encounter for this patient, it is likely world-level. If it is specific to one encounter, it is likely task-level. This guide covers world-level files only. If unsure, ask your pod lead.

### **I accidentally changed the World Spec template structure.**

Revert to the original template and re-enter your content. Engineering's pipeline reads the spec programmatically, so structural changes (renamed columns, rearranged sections, deleted headings) will break file generation. Compare your version to a clean copy of the template or ask your pod lead.

## **Self-QC**

### **I found a mismatch between my spec and my folder.**

Fix it before uploading. If a row in your spec has no matching file, produce or obtain the file. If a file in your folder has no matching row, either add the row to your spec or remove the file. Mismatches are the most common reason a package is returned for rework.

### **My file count does not match my row count.**

Walk through your spec row by row and check off each file as you find it in your folder. Identify which rows are missing files and which files are orphans. Fix each one. If a single row maps to two paired templates (e.g., discharge instructions plus medication list), both files count.

### **I am not sure if my package is complete.**

Run the self-QC checklist in Appendix C. If everything checks out, your package is complete. If you are still uncertain, share your folder and spec with your pod lead for a quick review before uploading.

## **RL Studio upload**

### **I cannot access RL Studio.**

Confirm you are using your Mercor expert email. If you still cannot log in, ask your pod lead to verify your access.

### **I do not know how to upload individual files.**

Refer to the RL Studio upload guide linked in Step 6\. If you are still stuck, ask your pod lead to walk you through it. Each file is a separate upload; do not package into a zip.

### **I uploaded the wrong files and need to fix my submission.**

Contact your pod lead immediately. They can advise whether you need to re-upload or whether the submission can be corrected in place.

### **I finished uploading. What do I do next?**

Post in your pod channel confirming the package is complete and tag your pod lead or reviewer. Engineering picks up the package from RL Studio and produces the synthetic files. You do not need to do anything further unless engineering or your reviewer comes back with questions.

## **General**

### **I am stuck and do not know who to ask.**

Your pod lead is your first point of contact for any question about the workflow. If your pod lead is unavailable, tag your reviewer. If neither responds within a reasonable time, escalate in the team-wide Slack channel.

### **I am confused about the overall workflow.**

Re-read Steps 1 through 6 at the top of this guide. The workflow is: brainstorm approved, draft spec, fill in file plan tables, use Claude to assemble templates, self-QC, upload to RL Studio. If a specific step is unclear, ask your pod lead to walk you through it.

### **This is my first world. Is there someone who can review my work before I submit?**

Yes. Your pod lead and reviewer are there to help, especially on your first world. Share your folder and spec with them before uploading to RL Studio. They can catch issues early and save you rework.

# 👣 Stage 1: Design the Patient and Clinical Scenario

## **Stage 1: Design the Patient and Clinical Scenario** 

**Fill this in World Spec Template → Section 1: Clinical Scenario**

This is where you define who your patient is and what happened to them. By the end of this section, a reader should understand your world in under 60 seconds.

## **1.1 Big Picture Summary**

Write a single paragraph summarizing the clinical world. Cover: the patient's primary presentation, the key complications that develop during the course, the core diagnostic or regulatory challenge the agent must navigate, and a high-level note on file set composition (e.g., "21 essential world-level files, 3 supplementary, 15 task-level").

A reader should be able to understand what this world tests — and why it is hard — without reading anything else.

## **1.2 Patient Profile**

Fill in the core demographic and clinical identity table. Keep the rows that apply to your scenario; add or remove rows as needed. Common fields include: name/DOB/age/sex, race/BMI (if clinically relevant), marital status/dependents, service or occupation, allergies/MRN, pre-existing conditions, and active problem list.

**Optional sub-tables.** Add any of the following directly under 1.2 if they add structural value to your world:

* **Home Medication List** — Include when the world tests medication reconciliation, polypharmacy, or prescribing decisions. Group by category (Cardiac, GI, Neuro, etc.) with dose, frequency, and indication. 15–30 medications is typical for medication-focused worlds.  
* **Hospital Course Timeline** — Include when the world involves a multi-day admission, perioperative sequence, or longitudinal care arc. Match granularity to the scenario.  
* **Decision Friction Table** — Include when the world has competing clinical or regulatory pathways the model must choose between. Use three columns: Friction Point | Options | Correct Pathway / Rationale.  
* **Data Hierarchy Note** — Include when sources conflict and the world tests whether the model applies the correct source-of-truth ranking (e.g., attending decision \> specialist consult \> progress note \> family/patient report \> EMR active orders).

## **1.3  Clinical History and Context**

Write a continuous narrative of the patient's clinical history. This is the authoritative clinical backstory that every task draws from. Cover: how the patient arrived at this point, the chronological progression of relevant conditions, key diagnostic workups and their results, surgical history, transitions of care, and the patient's current clinical status at the world snapshot date.

For regulatory or adjudication worlds, also cover the relevant regulatory history (prior claims, adjudications, appeals, service records) and the specific regulatory framework the tasks will reason against.

Every clinical fact referenced anywhere in the world (tasks, file plan, traps) should be traceable to this narrative or to a file in Section 3\. The narrative must be detailed enough that a file builder could generate any document from it alone.

## **1.4 Key Milestones**

Build a chronological table of every date and event that anchors the world. Every date referenced in tasks, traps, or file descriptions should appear here.

This is the **single source of truth for timeline consistency** — anything that doesn't appear in this table cannot be referenced elsewhere without creating an inconsistency. A complex world may have 15–25 milestone entries.

| Date | Event / Anchor |
| :---- | :---- |
| *\[Date\]* | *\[Event and its significance for the world design \- which trap or task it anchors\]* |

## **1.5 Clinical Complexity Overview**

Explain *why* this world is hard. This is not a restatement of the problem list — it is an analysis of why the combination of conditions, data, and context creates evaluation difficulty.

Address both clinical complexity (drug-drug interactions, multi-organ interplay, competing treatment goals) and any domain-specific complexity (regulatory layers, legal standards, coding ambiguity). A reader finishing this section should understand why an AI model would struggle with these tasks.

**Terminology — Traps vs. Frictions**

* **Traps** are informational obstacles in the source files (contradictory medication doses, buried significant findings, missing information requiring acknowledged uncertainty, source-of-truth ambiguity, temporal complexity, SDOH affecting reasoning).

* **Frictions** are people/perspective conflicts (specialty A vs. specialty B, family vs. clinical team, PCP vs. inpatient discharge, payer policy vs. clinical indication).

These are not interchangeable. Traps live in the data; frictions live in the relationships between stakeholders. A strong world has both.

# 👣 Stage 2: Design your Tasks

## **Stage 2: Design your Tasks**

**Fill this in World Spec Template → Section 2: Task Specifications**

# ---

**Section 2 Structure**

| The six fields below describe how the task is designed and evaluated. Only the Draft Prompt is sent to the AI agent. Workflow names, expected output structure, and trap reasoning are spec metadata — they help reviewers and graders, not the agent. Letting any of this leak into the prompt spoon-feeds the model and lowers our failure rate signal. |
| :---- |

For each task, complete the following five fields:

### **1\. Workflow**

What is happening and who is involved.   
E.g., *"OEM physician producing a nexus letter for a veteran's VA disability claim"* or *"Night float resident preparing discharge medication reconciliation."*

Refer to the [**Workflow List**](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1YRUwLm3oLjlL2v2g-_lw9rC_NeJ5gcpHBX6_M_HHh4c/edit?gid=668143205#gid=668143205) for approved workflows. Include a mix of clinical workflows (medication reconciliation, discharge summary, consult notes, pre-op clearance) and healthcare administration workflows (prior authorization, utilization review, E/M coding, HEDIS documentation). **At least one task must use a P0 workflow.**

### **2\. Draft Prompt**

Write the prompt in the voice of the clinician or user who would issue this request. Include the clinical context they would naturally provide, the documents they would attach, and any constraints they would mention. Keep it conversational and naturalistic — it should sound like a real request from a real person in a real workflow, not a test question or a rubric.

The anchor point (date, hospital day if inpatient) should be embedded in the prompt naturally — through the timestamp, the user's framing, or the documents attached.

### **3\. Expected Output**

Describe the deliverable: format, length, register, and the specific clinical content that constitutes a correct response. Name the key anchors the grader will check. This is the basis for the golden response. **If you cannot state the output precisely, the task is not ready.**

### **4\. Failure Design**

Document the **5–6 highest-yield traps** for this task in the Failure Design table. Each row has two columns: **Key Trap** (what misleads the model) and **Remediation** (what a correct response does instead and why). Full trap inventories with reasoning chains are maintained in your working spec; only the highest-yield traps appear in the spec doc.

For each trap, ask yourself: what is the plausible wrong answer, and why would a careful agent reach it? The remediation column should make explicit the reasoning chain that leads to the correct answer.

### **5\. Task-level files**

List any files scoped specifically to this task using the **E\#-T\# convention** — for example, `E1-T3` means the first essential file for Task 3\. If the task uses only world-level files, write *"None. World-level files only."* If a file is shared across multiple tasks, note the reuse. Reuse does not violate task independence because tasks are graded as separate evaluation runs.

---

**Design Standards**

Before moving to your world spec, check your brainstorm against these standards.

| What You Do | Where It Goes |
| :---- | :---- |
|  **Target at least 15–20 files per world** | Your world should contain at least 15–20 clinical documents. This is enough to create a realistic chart environment where the agent must navigate and locate relevant information. Fewer than 15 files usually means the scenario is not complex enough; significantly more than 20 may make the world unwieldy to review and maintain. |
| **Plan your traps during brainstorm, not after** | Traps should be woven into the clinical scenario from the start — they are part of the patient's story, not additions layered on afterward. During brainstorm, identify where in the clinical timeline conflicting information, subtle errors, or ambiguous decision points would naturally occur. If you design the scenario first and try to add traps later, they tend to feel artificial and are easier for the agent to detect. |
| **Traps must require cross-referencing** | A trap that lives in a single document — one wrong lab value, one contradictory date — is a weak trap. Strong traps span multiple files and require the agent to synthesize information across documents to catch the issue. For example: a medication dosage change documented in a pharmacy note but not reflected in the discharge medication list, where the agent must reconcile both sources to produce an accurate reconciliation. |
| **Build for complexity**  | Your patient scenario should involve multiple comorbidities, at least one significant complication or clinical turning point, and consultations from more than one specialty. A straightforward admission-to-discharge with a single diagnosis does not generate enough material for challenging tasks. |
| **Formatting follows EMR conventions** |  The generated files will follow the formatting style of major EMR systems (Epic, Cerner). You do not need to format your spec to look like an EMR — but when you describe what a document should contain, think in terms of how that document would actually appear in an EMR. Progress notes have a specific structure. Lab reports have a specific layout. Engineering's synthetic generation pipeline handles the actual formatting, so your spec should reflect realistic clinical documentation patterns. |

# 👣 Stage 3a: Build the File Plan

## **Stage 3: Build the File Plan** 

**Fill this in [World Spec Template](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1KT7TjQi18RQKqcZNOuwrtziX1w_V-Pd5/edit) → Section 3: World File Plan**

| The World File Plan is part of the World Spec document that gets uploaded to RL Studio at Step 4 of the pipeline, together with your Reference Templates folder. Once World Spec Human Review (Step 6\) signs off, engineering's synthetic generation pipeline auto-extracts the spec and the Reference Templates folder to produce the world files at Step 7\. The dedicated Writer Guide for Reference Templates walks through the curation workflow. |
| :---- |

# ---

The full file inventory lives in **Section 3 (World File Plan)**, organized into three subsections:

|  | Essential *(required for at least one task; may carry trap content)* | Supplementary *(realistic noise; must NOT carry trap content)* |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **World-Level** *(visible to all tasks)* | The base clinical environment — chart, labs, medication lists, consult notes that any task may reference.  | Realism additions visible to all tasks.  |
| **Task-Level** *(scoped to specific tasks)* | Task-specific input not in the longitudinal chart — referring physician email, prior authorization form, RCA meeting minutes.  | Realism additions scoped to specific tasks.   |

Aim for approximately **90% essential / 10% supplementary across the world as a whole** — combining all four file types (essential world-level, essential task-level, supplementary world-level, supplementary task-level). Every file should exist either because a task requires it (essential) or because it adds realistic clinical noise (supplementary). If removing a file would not change any correct answer and adds no noise value, remove it.

**File descriptions must be detailed enough for a non-domain-expert builder to draft.** "Standard progress note" is not enough. Specify the key clinical content, the structure, any specific findings or language that must be included, and where trap content should appear. Vague descriptions produce unusable files — and that costs you revision cycles.

# ---

All three subsections in Section 3 use the same eight-column structure. To ensure alignment, here is what each column should contain:

| Column | What goes in it |
| :---: | ----- |
| **\#** | Sequential row number within the subsection. Restart numbering at the top of each subsection (3.1, 3.2, 3.3). |
| **ID** | We recommend using the following naming convention for individual files:  **EW\# for essential world\-level files.** For example, if you have 35 essential world files, then you should accordingly assign the following IDs: *EW1, EW2, EW3, EW4…EW35.*  **WS\# for world\-level supplementary files.** For example, if you have 3 supplementary files (for cognitive noise, but contains no traps), then you should assign them the following identifiers: WS1, WS2, and WS3  **E\#-T\# for essential files at the task\-level.** Let’s say Task 1 has two essential files at the task level. They should be named *E1-T1* and *E2-T1* respectively. Or if Task 7 has only 1 essential file, then its ID should be *E1-T7*. |
| **Filename.type** | The full filename, ideally including a date stamp in `MMDDYYYY` format and the file extension. Example: `DischargeSummary_04262026.docx`.  |
| **Date** | The date should match a date listed in the **Section 1.4 Key Milestones** timeline table in the [World Spec Template](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1KT7TjQi18RQKqcZNOuwrtziX1w_V-Pd5/edit). Even if redundant with the filename.type, you should still include it. |
| **Reference File Origin** | Three options: **A) Public Domain** — use an existing publicly available document *If your document is a form/document that is publicly available online (e.g. FMLA form), then simply type something along the lines of **“Public Domain (FMLA Form: Dept. of Labor).”](https://docs.google.com/document/d/13tOzO_0RdOXjPV8268oUErxzR0B3Ie_w/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=111631573631761265982&rtpof=true&sd=true)*  [**B) Databank of templates (internal)](https://docs.google.com/document/d/13tOzO_0RdOXjPV8268oUErxzR0B3Ie_w/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=111631573631761265982&rtpof=true&sd=true)** — use Mercor's internal template library Use the link above to see the many types of clinical templates the team leads have compiled. The standardized workflow is to use the Claude Project setup described in the Writer Guide for Reference Templates. The guide walks you through pulling templates from the DataBank into your Reference Templates folder, deciding the source for any row the DataBank does not cover, and packaging everything for upload to RL Studio at Step 4\. **C) Custom made by writer** — you create from scratch when neither A nor B applies.  *Maybe you want to simulate a **handwritten list of medications** by a caregiver and take a photo of it. Or if you want to record a **mock conversation** between a patient and a physician and upload it as an audio world file.  Whichever the case, simply let the receiving team know that they do NOT need to bother synthetically generating this for you (e.g. **“Custom made (handwritten list of meds).**”* |
| **Description** | Detailed specification of what the file should contain: clinical content to include, clinical content to exclude, and format/layout requirements. Detailed enough that a non-domain-expert builder could draft it. *"Standard progress note"* is not enough — specify key clinical content, structure, and any specific findings or language that must be included. |
| **Pearls, Traps, and Friction** | Two-part annotation: **Part 1 — Pearls:** What does this file accomplish in the patient narrative? What is its function in the chart? What clinical pearls should a physician reading this learn? **Part 2 — Traps and Friction:** What trap content (if any) is embedded in this file? What stakeholder frictions does it surface? Reference back to the relevant traps in the Failure Design tables in Section 2\. |

## **Working with the Engineering Pipeline**

You write the specification and curate the Reference Templates folder; engineering's pipeline produces the files. Once the World Spec Human Review gate (Step 6\) signs off on your spec and Reference Templates together, engineering's pipeline automatically extracts them and starts synthetic generation. There is no manual handoff.

**How file generation works**

The pipeline produces standard generalist documents: progress notes, lab reports, nursing flowsheets, medication lists, imaging reports, and similar standard clinical documents.

Specialized clinical files requiring physician expertise (custom EKG tracings, ventilator waveforms, complex clinical decision support outputs) still require Team Lead approval before you create them yourself.

Once the world clears Writer File Review (Step 9), the world is locked. World-level files do not change after locking. Task-level adjustments are handled at the task level.

**Reviewing generated files**

After engineering generates the files, World AutoQC (Step 8\) runs automatically on file integrity, schema, and world consistency. If AutoQC fails, the pipeline loops back to Step 7 to regenerate.

Once AutoQC passes, the files are released to you for Writer File Review (Step 9). Your job:

* Verify clinical content (dates, names, doses, consistency across documents).

* Confirm intended trap content survived generation.

* Identify and correct any new inconsistencies or errors.

Two paths depending on issue size:

* Minor issues (small edits across a few documents) \- edit in place inside RL Studio.

* Major issues (more than \~1/3 of documents require substantial edits, broken schemas, missing files, or systemic spec misinterpretation) \- resubmit to engineering to regenerate. This loops back to Step 7\.

* 

**For images, audio, and other custom artifacts, you generate these yourself or source reputable, publicly available materials.**

⚠️ NOTE: It is critical that your traps are integrated into your synthetic files in a 'reasonably ambiguous' fashion (not glaringly obvious) so that the clinical complexity remains while still considered fair game for any seasoned physician expert to solve. For example, if a trap implies the patient is prediabetic in a progress note, the HPI should state the patient had an A1c of 5.8%, not blatantly say 'Mr. Jones is prediabetic.'

File naming. Keep it simple and intuitive. Avoid overly detailed naming conventions. Simpler names help the model understand and look up information more effectively.

Every essential file in the spec should include either a reference document link with usage instructions, or a description detailed enough for a non-domain-expert builder to draft it. 'Standard progress note' is not enough. Specify key clinical content, structure, and any specific findings or language that must be included.

**File naming** \- Keep it simple and intuitive. Avoid overly detailed naming conventions. Simpler names help the model understand and look up information more effectively.

## 

## **Clinical File design tactics**

* **Include dates in all file names and within the documents themselves**  
  For example, `progress_note_day3_02152026.pdf`. This is essential for temporal anchoring across tasks.

* **Establish a data hierarchy.** Document this in your world spec and reference it when traps depend on source priority: *attending decision \> specialist consult \> progress note \> transfer note \> patient/family report.*

* **Avoid over-authoritative summaries.** If your world contains a document that synthesizes everything — a prior clinical summary, an old discharge summary — make it outdated, incomplete, or wrong in a material respect. A world where a single document tells the agent everything it needs removes the need for reasoning.

* **No single file should resolve any task without cross-referencing at least one other file.** If it does, the task does not require multi-document reasoning and has limited benchmarking value.

* **Calibrate trap visibility after files are generated.** Trap design isn't finished at the spec stage. Once the synthetic files come back, review every embedded trap to confirm it is **buried enough** that the model can plausibly miss it, but **discoverable enough** that a seasoned clinician working through the chart carefully would arrive at the correct decision. Two failure modes to fix before the world is locked:

* **Too obvious** — any model picks it up; the trap stops differentiating. Bury the cue deeper or distribute it across more documents.  
* **Not fair game** — even a seasoned expert wouldn't find it. Surface the cue more, or split it across two findable locations the agent can triangulate.

# 🧑‍🏫 Stage 3b: Template Curation Tutorial

**Template/Reference File Curation Guide**

Template and Reference File Workflow

See below for our guidance regarding the template/reference file workflow. If you get stuck on any step, ping your pod lead in Slack.

## **Types of world-level files you will encounter**

Before diving into the steps, here is a quick reference for the four types of files and who handles what:

| Category | Who creates it | Engineering converts? | Examples |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| DataBank template | Claude extracts from the DataBank verbatim | Yes | Progress note, discharge summary, consult note, H\&P |
| Custom-made template | Writer drafts (Claude can help). Still a template, not a final file. | Yes | Institution-specific pre-op template, hospital P\&L Excel template, specialty clinic note format |
| Public domain form | Writer downloads the official blank form from the source agency | Yes (fills and converts) | FMLA form (Dept. of Labor), USCIS I-693 immigration physical, OSHA injury log |
| Writer-produced file (not a template) | Writer creates the actual finalized file using specialty tools | No (already done) | Custom EKG tracing (clinical data simulator), pill bottle photo (NanoBanana Pro), ambient scribe audio (ElevenLabs) |

| Key takeaway. The first three categories are templates/forms that engineering will convert into realistic synthetic files. The fourth category is the small number of files you finalize yourself because they require your clinical domain expertise. All four categories get uploaded to RL Studio together. |
| :---- |

You cannot draft a spec without an approved brainstorm. Post your brainstorm checkpoint in your pod channel and tag your lead. Wait for approval before moving on.

## **🌐 Public Domain Files**

While **public-domain images** are permitted, please ensure all embedded metadata is scrubbed prior to submission. A simple method is to capture a **screenshot** of the asset (using Snipping Tool or Cmd+Shift+4) and utilize that version. To maintain compliance, **avoid copying and pasting directly from web sources**.

We recommend sourcing images from **reputable medical or educational repositories**. This includes governmental and academic bodies (e.g., NIH, CDC, WHO) or established open-access platforms like **Life in the Fast Lane (LITFL)** and **Radiopaedia**, provided the specific file is licensed for reuse.

Assets must be verified for reuse (e.g., public domain or Creative Commons). To ensure high-fidelity compliance, verify the licensing terms on the source site—specifically searching for labels such as **“public domain”** or **“CC BY-SA.”** If the licensing status is ambiguous, please refrain from using the image.

When in doubt, **err on the side of caution** and select an alternative source.

# 🧬 Stage 3e: Synthetic Clinical Data Generators

## **How to Use Our Custom Clinical Data Generators**

## 

To help you create high-fidelity clinical data without using real patient information, we have developed and curated a set of **custom synthetic data generators**. These browser-based tools allow you to generate publication-quality mock clinical documents and waveforms for your world file sets.

| Tool | What It Generates | Use Case | Link |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| EEG Simulator | Synthetic EEG tracings with configurable montages, waveforms, and abnormalities | Neuro, epilepsy, ICU, and status epilepticus scenarios | [EEG Teaching Sim](https://kingpascual1992-cmd.github.io/eegteachingsim/) |
| EKG Simulator | 12-lead EKG tracings with configurable rhythms, intervals, and pathology | Cardiology, ED, pre-op, and inpatient scenarios | [EKG Simulator](https://kingpascual1992-cmd.github.io/ekgsimulatordoc/) |
| EFM Simulator | Electronic fetal monitoring strips with configurable patterns and decelerations | OB/GYN, L\&D triage, and intrapartum monitoring scenarios | [EFM Simulator (OB/GYN)](https://kingpascual1992-cmd.github.io/efmsimulatorobgyn/) |
| Ventilator Simulator (Option 1\) | Ventilator waveform displays with configurable modes and parameters | ICU, pulmonary, respiratory failure, and ventilator management scenarios | [RT Maven Vent Sim](https://sim.rtmaven.com/) |
| Ventilator Simulator (Option 2\) | Alternative ventilator parameter and waveform generator | ICU, pulmonary, and weaning protocol scenarios | [MedData Vent Sim](https://med-data-nine.vercel.app/) |
| Lab Report Simulator | Formatted laboratory reports with configurable values, reference ranges, and panels | Any scenario requiring realistic lab documentation | [MedData Lab Sim](https://med-data-nine.vercel.app/) |
| Radiology Report Simulator | Structured radiology reports with configurable findings, impressions, and recommendations | Any scenario requiring imaging reports (CT, MRI, X-ray, Ultrasound) | [MedData Radiology Sim](https://med-data-nine.vercel.app/) |
| Sample Lab Reports (Reference) | Real-world lab report formatting and reference ranges from LabCorp’s test menu | Reference for formatting and normal ranges when building custom lab files | [LabCorp Test Menu](https://www.labcorp.com/test-menu/search) |

![][image32]

### ![][image33]![][image34]

### **How to Use the Generators in Your Workflow**

1. **Identify the clinical data needed.** Review your World Spec and task prompts. What documents would realistically exist at each task’s timepoint?

2. **Configure the simulator.** Open the appropriate tool and set parameters to match your patient’s clinical scenario.

3. **Export and annotate.** Export the generated file. Add a text-based interpretation or report that accompanies the visual data.

4. **Embed traps in the data.** Clinical data files are prime trap locations (e.g., a borderline prolonged QTc when the patient is about to start a QT-prolonging medication).

5. **Obtain approval for specialized files.** Confirm with your team lead before including specialized waveform or imaging files.

### **Tool Use: Clinical Calculators & Real-Time Search**

Some tasks should test whether the AI agent can appropriately **use external tools** as part of its clinical reasoning. Examples:

* **Clinical risk calculators:** A task requiring the agent to calculate a HEART score using data scattered across multiple documents.

* **Drug interaction checks:** A medication list with a subtle but clinically significant interaction the agent should flag unprompted.

* **Real-time web search:** A task where the correct answer depends on current clinical guidelines that differ from older guidelines embedded in the chart.

* **Literature retrieval:** A task requiring the agent to cite a specific clinical trial or guideline to justify a treatment recommendation.

| Design principle: Tool use should never be the entire task — it should be one component of a larger clinical workflow. The agent should recognize when a tool is needed, use it correctly, and integrate the result into its clinical reasoning. |
| :---- |

### **O*nly files and images available in the public domain are permitted for use. Please ensure all materials are free of copyright restrictions before using them.***

# 👣 Stage 4: Additional References (Optional)

## **Stage 4: Additional References (Optional)** 

This section is for any supporting material your world needs that doesn't fit in Sections 1–3. Not every world will require all of these — include only what is necessary for file builders and task designers to maintain consistency.

##  **Common additions**

**Key Facts Reference Sheet** 

A standalone consistency-checking document for file builders. Include every fixed fact that must remain consistent across all files: patient demographics, care team names and credentials, baseline lab values, key dates, medication timeline, and clinical milestones. A fact is "key" if changing it would break a task, neutralize a trap, or create an internal inconsistency. Cross-reference your key facts against your trap designs to make sure the facts each trap depends on are locked in here and not left to builder discretion.

**Embedded Conflicts**

A log of every deliberate contradiction you have designed into the world: which documents conflict, what each says, and which version is correct. This serves two purposes: it gives file builders explicit instructions on what contradictions to preserve (not "fix"), and it gives you a master list to audit against when reviewing generated files. If a file builder encounters a contradiction not on this list, it's a bug. If it's on this list, it's intentional.

**Daily Clinical Reference**

Vital signs, laboratory values, and key clinical events for each hospital day. This is the **source of truth** for per-day clinical data when generating progress notes, nursing notes, and consultant notes. If your world has a multi-day hospitalization, this table prevents drift between what different files say happened on the same day.

**Key Laboratory Trends**

Longitudinal lab values at key timepoints across the hospitalization. Use this when your traps depend on the agent correctly interpreting lab trends (e.g., a creatinine that rises from 1.2 to 3.8 and then partially recovers, affecting medication dosing decisions at different timepoints).

**Specialist Friction**

A structured record of where specialist assessments diverge, what each service recommends, and how the attending resolves the disagreement. Use this when your world includes specialist friction traps so that file builders know exactly which recommendations to put in which consult notes.

**Clinical Documentation Style Guide** (World Spec Template)

Voice and formatting rules for each document type in your world (attending notes, ED notes, consult notes, nursing notes, lab reports, imaging, orders, policies). Use this when your world requires a consistent house style across documents — particularly useful if multiple file builders will work on the same world.

**Other world-specific reference tables** as needed. 

If your world has unique reference needs (e.g., a medication conversion table, an insurance formulary, a facility-specific policy), add them as doc subsections.

**Relationship to Section 1**

Several of the optional subsections you may have added in Section 1 (Home Medication List, Hidden Clinical Finding, Specialist Friction, Key Laboratory Trends, Embedded Conflicts, Timeline) overlap with or cross-reference the tabs listed here. The Section 1 subsections provide the narrative context — what the clinical situation is and why it matters. The Section 4 / OTHER REFERENCES tabs provide the structured data — the specific values and facts that file builders need to implement your design.

# 😮 Common Mistakes

## **Common Mistakes in World Spec Docs**

| Mistake | Why It’s a Problem |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Letting blueprint content leak into the prompt** | Of the six task fields in Section 2, only the **Draft Prompt** becomes the user message the agent receives. Workflow, Expected Output, Failure Design, and the file ID list are spec metadata for reviewers, graders, and engineering. The prompt should sound like a real user request, not hand the agent context (workflow labels, output structure, trap hints, *"note: some documents may be outdated"*) that it should derive from the files. Spoon-feeding the model lowers the failure rate signal. |
| **Leaving required sections incomplete** | Sections 1.1–1.4, Section 2 (overview paragraph), and Section 3 must all be filled. For optional subsections (1.x, Section 4), omit them entirely if they don't apply — do not leave placeholder text. |
| **Designing files before tasks** | Files exist to support tasks. Finish all task designs first, then ask: what files does each task require? |
| **Writing prompts that hint at the trap** | The prompt should sound like a real clinical request. "Check for errors in the medication list" gives it away. The agent should discover problems by reading the documents carefully. |
| **Leaving the hidden finding vague** | "The case is complex" is not a finding. State exactly what the agent must discover, which files contain the evidence, and what synthesis is required. |
| **Putting trap content in supplementary files** | Supplementary files add realism and noise only. If a file contains trap content or information critical to a task, it belongs in Essential. |
| **Including over-authorative summaries** | If a single document synthesizes everything the agent needs — a complete discharge summary, a prior clinical summary — make it outdated, incomplete, or wrong in a material respect. Otherwise the agent can answer correctly without cross-referencing, and the task loses benchmarking value. |
| **Not specifying reference documents for essential files** | Every essential file should include either a reference file link or a description detailed enough for a non-clinician builder to produce a realistic draft. |
| **A single file resolves a task** | If one essential file contains everything the agent needs for a task, no cross-document reasoning is required. Every task should require synthesis across at least two files. |
